title: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical neurons from monozygotic twins with the Gαo1 K278del mutation reveal disease mechanisms relevant to GNAO1-related encephalopathy.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Rare de novo variants in GNAO1 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a heterogenous display of early onset epilepsy, movement abnormalities, and global developmental delay. More than 100 pathogenic variants in GNAO1 have been identified and categorized into four groups according to their protein features. Most pathogenic variants affect both GNAO1 isoforms, whereas approximately 20% of patients have a GNAO1A-specific variant. Response to therapy is notoriously variable, even among patients harboring the same variant. Here, we set out to model GNAO1A-related encephalopathy using human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) from monozygotic twins carrying the Gαo1 K278del variant and uncovered-while taking advantage of the identical genomic setting-phenotypic features that further our understanding of the defects underlying the disorder. METHODS: We generated hiPSCs expressing the c.832_834delAAG; p.K278del variant in GNAO1A obtained from monozygotic twins who both developed seizures 2 days after birth. For either twin, Gαo1 K278del and CRISPR-Cas9-repaired isogenic control hiPSC lines were differentiated into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and subsequently into cortical neurons. Variant-specific transcriptomic, morphological, and electrophysiological characteristics were analyzed. RESULTS: Gαo1 K278del mutated hiPSC-derived NPCs showed disorganized neural rosette structures and revealed an altered transcriptome. In cortical neurons, the Gαo1 K278del variant caused a reduction in the size and complexity of dendrites that was accompanied by an increase in pre- and postsynaptic puncta. Multielectrode array (MEA) recordings revealed an abnormal cortical neuron bursting activity pattern with fewer bursts and more spikes per burst. The antiepileptic drug levetiracetam reduced the spike frequency and the number of spikes per burst in cortical neurons from both patients. SIGNIFICANCE: The developed GNAO1A hiPSC-derived in vitro model uncovered key structural and functional features of GNAO1-related encephalopathy. The comparable in vitro phenotypes in neurons from both twins underscore the utility of hiPSC-derived models to investigate molecular mechanisms underlying GNAO1-related encephalopathy as well as effects of therapeutic intervention.

title: Tubulin polyglutamylation modulates Golgi morphodynamics and neurite branching during neuronal morphogenesis.
abstract: Neurons establish functional networks through morphological remodeling during neuronal differentiation. Microtubule polyglutamylation is a key microtubule post-translational modification that is highly enriched during this process and plays an important role in differentiation. However, how remodeling of organelle features such as morphology, distribution and interactions depends on tubulin polyglutamylation during neuronal differentiation remains unclear. Here, we employed multispectral imaging combined with quantitative three-dimensional organelle analysis to comprehensively profile eight organelles simultaneously in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons. We discovered that depletion of tubulin polyglutamylation induces pronounced alterations in somatic Golgi morphology and associated organelle interactions. In addition, Golgi-derived compartments in proximal neurites exhibited altered morphology and dynamics, namely, decreased anterograde transport together with less efficient movement. These changes were accompanied by increased neurite branching and tortuosity. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for tubulin polyglutamylation in coordinating organelle organization with neurite architecture, providing a mechanistic link between tubulin post-translational modifications, Golgi morphology, dynamics and neuronal morphogenesis.

title: Analysis of motor-based transport in primary cilia by dynamic mode decomposition of live-cell imaging data.
abstract: Kinesin-3 motor proteins are increasingly recognized for their important roles in cilia. The mammalian kinesin-3 motor KIF13B moves bidirectionally in primary cilia and regulates ciliary content, but its relationship to the intraflagellar transport (IFT) machinery is unclear. Here, we combine quantitative live-cell imaging with a new kymograph analysis based on dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to separate mobile from immobile protein populations in primary cilia. This approach simplifies extraction of molecular velocities from kymographs and improves directional analysis of molecular tracks using the Fourier and Radon transforms. Our novel analysis reveals that a KIF13B deletion mutant only retaining the motor domain and part of the forkhead-associated domain does not alter steady-state IFT velocity or frequency. However, when retrograde dynein-2 function is inhibited by ciliobrevin D or tanespimycin, both anterograde and retrograde IFT velocities decrease in parental cells, as expected, but remain unchanged in KIF13B mutant cells. Structured illumination, confocal and stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy further show that KIF13B localizes to the ciliary membrane and concentrates at the periciliary membrane region and the centriolar subdistal appendages, below the distal appendage marker FBF1. Our improved kymograph approach provides new insight into KIF13B ciliary function and simplifies the quantitative analysis of ciliary protein transport.

title: Extracting Patterns from Developmental Microscopy Data: Cell States and Behaviors, Trajectories, Deformations, and Networks.
abstract: Embryonic development is remarkable in its reproducibility: across individuals, cells repeatedly organize in space and time to build complex tissues and structures. Identifying such recurring organization is a central aim of biological research because it reveals constraints that any mechanistic explanation of development must satisfy. Modern microscopy can now follow the formation of whole organisms at cellular or subcellular resolution over long periods, generating four-dimensional, multichannel movies that contain far more information than can be reliably identified and compared by eye. The challenge is therefore not simply to observe development, but to extract from these movies patterns that are reproducible, comparable, and mechanistically informative. Here we review computational strategies for pattern extraction from developmental and morphogenetic imaging, with selected adjacent studies used as methodological examples. We synthesize the literature through four complementary views-cell states and behaviors, cell and nuclear trajectories, tissue deformation, and cellular networks and topology. Across these studies, the same questions recur: What biological object should be represented? When should two observations count as similar? What evidence establishes that an apparent pattern is reproducible? We connect primary examples to representative methods and formal definitions, emphasizing biological scale, inputs, outputs, assumptions, and limitations. By making recurring developmental organization measurable and comparable, these approaches turn increasingly rich movies into quantitative constraints on mechanism.

title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1-3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this 'female protective effect' (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

title: Bioinformatic investigation of convergent proteins and cellular functions downstream of autism-associated genes.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder affects 1 in 31 people yet exhibits remarkable genetic heterogeneity with over 1000 genes identified in autistic populations producing convergent neurobiological phenotypes through not yet understood mechanisms. Here, we employed systems-level network analysis to test if diverse autism risk genes converge onto common cellular vulnerabilities across brain cell types. Using 1238 autism-associated genes from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) database, we stratified genes by cell-type-specific expression patterns and constructed protein-protein interaction networks to map functional clusters and identify critical connector proteins. Through permutation-based statistical analysis, we identified convergent downstream proteins targets, representing molecular vulnerabilities where multiple autism-associated protein pathways converge for miscoordination of cellular function. Network analysis revealed cell-type-specific vulnerability signatures: SYN1 in inhibitory neurons, GRIN/DLG/CAMK2 proteins in excitatory neurons, GRIA2A/DLG4/GRIN2 in oligodendrocyte precursor cells, ACTL6B in oligodendrocytes, and ARHGAP/DOCK proteins in astrocytes. Remarkably, these computationally predicted targets have been independently validated in human genetics and autism research, demonstrating that network-based convergent vulnerability analysis successfully identifies critical nodes where diverse genetic insults disrupt coordinated cellular responses. This framework provides a molecular basis for understanding autism pathophysiology and identifies promising targets for intervention in the treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Cell Type-Specific Assessment of Cholesterol Distribution in Models of Neurodevelopmental Disorders.
abstract: Most nervous system disorders manifest through alterations in neuronal signaling based on abnormalities in neuronal excitability, synaptic transmission, and cell survival. However, such neuronal phenotypes are frequently accompanied or even caused by metabolic dysfunctions in neuronal or non-neuronal cells. The tight packing and highly heterogeneous properties of neural, glial, and vascular cell types pose significant challenges to dissecting metabolic aspects of brain disorders. Perturbed cholesterol homeostasis has recently emerged as a key parameter associated with subsets of neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegeneration. However, approaches for tracking and visualizing endogenous cholesterol distribution in the brain have limited capability of resolving cell type-specific differences. We here develop tools for genetically encoded sensors that report on accessible cholesterol distribution in the mouse brain with cellular resolution. We apply these probes to examine subcellular cholesterol accumulation in two genetic mouse models of brain disorders, male Ptchd1 knock-out and male and female Npc1 knock-out mice. While both genes encode proteins with sterol-sensing domains that have been implicated in cholesterol transport, we uncover highly selective and cell type-specific phenotypes in cholesterol homeostasis. The tools established in this work should facilitate probing subcellular cholesterol distribution in complex tissues like the mammalian brain and enable capturing cell type-specific alterations in cholesterol flow between cells in models of brain disorders.

title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Conditional Mutant MAPT Overexpression in Neural Organoids Elicits Robust Tau Accumulation and Pathological Transcriptomic Responses.
abstract: Modeling neurodegenerative conditions in neural organoids presents a potential complement to existing preclinical translation pipelines. Prior neural organoid models have generally relied on human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines containing disease-relevant alleles. However, this strategy limits temporal control over the initiation and progression of pathological events. In this study, we provide a proof-of-concept framework showing that neurodegenerative phenotypes can be triggered by inducible expression cassettes. We developed an iPSC line harboring doxycycline-inducible mutant MAPT, which encodes the microtubule-associated protein tau that is implicated in tauopathies. Induction of mutant MAPT via doxycycline treatment in differentiating neural organoids yielded accumulation of phosphorylated tau, which localized inside individual neuron somas within the cortical plate-like regions. Importantly, measured transcriptomic responses to tau overexpression bore key similarities to human clinical transcriptomic data. Taken together, we present an approach for controlling the initiation and progression of proteinopathy-like pathology in neural organoid systems.

title: Migraine-driven causal genes in ischemic stroke.
abstract: Migraine, most notably migraine with aura, elevates the risk of ischaemic stroke, though the underlying causal molecular connections have not been fully elucidated. This study sought to uncover migraine-associated causal genes that confer susceptibility to ischaemic stroke and to dissect their cell-type-specific functional mechanisms operating within the neurovascular unit. We combined publicly available human transcriptomic resources, genetics-driven causal inference, machine-learning-assisted biomarker screening, mouse-derived single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlases, immune-cell deconvolution, and in-silico molecular docking. Twenty migraine-related genes were detected with causal associations to ischaemic-stroke risk. We prioritised three consensus hub genes: CD79A, PKN2, and PRKDC. In stroke patients, CD79A was significantly downregulated, while PKN2 and PRKDC exhibited elevated expression; their reliable diagnostic capacity was further confirmed in an independent external cohort. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiling mapped these hub genes to endothelial, myeloid and glial cell populations residing within a dynamic inflammatory-vascular pathological niche in mouse ischaemic brain lesions. Mechanistic analyses pointed to perturbed mitochondrial energy homeostasis and dysregulated adaptive immune responses as downstream consequences modulated by these hub genes. Molecular-docking simulations demonstrated high-affinity interactions between Tamibarotene, Dirithromycin and the three encoded hub proteins, highlighting these compounds as promising candidates for drug repurposing. Collectively, our multi-omics analysis pinpoints CD79A, PKN2 and PRKDC as migraine-derived causal targets for ischaemic stroke, delivers cell- and spatial-resolved mechanistic perspectives on neurovascular-unit injury, and puts forward lead compounds awaiting further pre-clinical validation.

title: Protein Isoaspartate Repair in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: An Integrative Bioinformatic Analysis of the PCMT Gene Family.
abstract: Protein homeostasis is a fundamental determinant of neuronal survival, and its disruption contributes to the pathogenesis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Protein L-isoaspartate O-methyltransferases (PCMTs) are evolutionarily conserved proteins involved in the recognition and processing of damaged proteins through the repair of isoaspartyl residues and protein quality-control pathways; however, their potential involvement in ALS remains largely unexplored. Here, we performed a comprehensive in silico characterization of the PCMT family (PCMT1, PCMTD1, and PCMTD2) by integrating structural, transcriptomic, single-cell, genetic, and protein modeling analyses. Domain analysis demonstrated that all three proteins share a conserved PCMT domain, while predicted S-adenosylmethionine-binding motifs were identified in PCMT1 and PCMTD2 but not PCMTD1, indicating evolutionary conservation with functional divergence. Expression profiling revealed that PCMT family genes are expressed in ALS-relevant tissues and broadly distributed across neuronal, glial, vascular, and immune cell populations in both healthy and ALS-associated brain single-cell data sets. Analysis of multiple independent ALS transcriptomic cohorts identified consistent upregulation of PCMT family members, with PCMTD1 exhibiting the most reproducible disease-associated expression changes across nervous system tissues and peripheral blood. Gene set correlation analyses further revealed distinct relationships between PCMT expression and neuronal pathways, with PCMT1 showing positive associations with axonal transport and synaptic signaling, whereas PCMTD1 and PCMTD2 displayed largely inverse correlation patterns. Rare missense variants identified in ALS patients were predicted to impair protein function and decrease protein stability, while structural modeling suggested that several substitutions may disrupt conserved residues and the local protein architecture. Collectively, these findings identify the PCMT family as previously underexplored candidates associated with ALS and provide a comprehensive framework for future mechanistic studies investigating their roles in neuronal protein homeostasis and neurodegeneration.

title: Transcriptomic signature of frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 type C pathology.
abstract: The semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia is a clinical subtype of frontotemporal lobar degeneration and is marked by TDP-43 subtype C pathology (FTLD-TDP C). It is a sporadic disease, yet has a strikingly homogeneous clinicopathological presentation, suggesting a common pathophysiology. The aim of this study was to discover dysregulated pathways in FTLD-TDP C through transcriptomics of the temporal cortex-its most affected region. Bulk RNA sequencing was conducted on temporal cortices of a post-mortem cohort of 18 FTLD-TDP C patients and 23 sex- and age-matched controls. Differential expression and functional analyses were performed to identify differentially expressed genes [DEGs; false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05] and functionally annotate them. We assessed the enrichment of TARDBP's protein interactors and RNA targets among the DEGs. Our findings were compared with other published RNA sequencing data on tauopathies (Alzheimer's dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy and FTLD with MAPT), FTLD-TDP (subtypes A and B) and available proteomics from this cohort. Additionally, we performed a weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), adjusting for differences in cell type composition between cases and controls using cell deconvolution, and removing genes dysregulated in temporal cortices identified in other datasets. Among the FTLD-TDP DEGs, we focused on the enrichment of synaptic processes using SynGO. We found upregulation of (i) damage response, (ii) cell structure and (iii) RNA splicing processes, and (iv) downregulation of synaptic processes in 6322 DEGs and five disease-related WGCNA modules. TARDBP-related genes were enriched among the DEGs. Additionally, transmembrane transport across the neurovascular unit was dysregulated. After cell deconvolution and removal of common tau genes, postsynaptic processes remained dysregulated, specifically the gene ontology terms 'modulation of chemical synaptic transmission' and 'neurotransmitter receptor localization to postsynaptic specialization membrane'. We found 11 synaptic FTLD-TDP C-specific genes affected at both the RNA and protein levels in the temporal cortex, which were involved in synaptic adhesion (CADM1, NCAN), signal transmission (COMT, RGS144, SLC1A2, TUBB2B) and synaptic plasticity (BEGAIN, ITPKA, LRFN1, RAB3B, SYNPO). In conclusion, a wide range of processes were dysregulated at the RNA level in the temporal cortex of FTLD-TDP C, including commonly affected processes in neurodegeneration, such as structural cell alterations. Dysregulation of TARDBP-related genes and RNA splicing has also been observed in other TDP-43 proteinopathies. Importantly, we found that postsynaptic processes were downregulated in FTLD-TDP C, after removing tauopathy-related genes and after cell deconvolution. In particular, the assembly of receptors at the postsynaptic membrane and synaptic signal transmission were affected, both at the RNA and protein levels. Future research on these pathways could elucidate distinct pathophysiological mechanisms and guide targeted clinical approaches.

title: Comprehensive classification of HCN1 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with and without epilepsy.
abstract: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 1 (HCN1) channels mediate the cationic Ih current, a fundamental regulator of neuronal excitability and synaptic integration, and are predominantly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus. Although HCN1 variants have been increasingly identified in patients with epilepsy, from milder forms to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE), genotype-phenotype correlations remain poorly defined. Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology and confocal imaging in HEK293 cells to functionally characterize 43 HCN1 variants identified in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders, with or without epilepsy. Based on biophysical properties, we established a classification system comprising four distinct functional classes: I) low or no current; II) hyperpolarizing shift in voltage dependence; III) depolarizing shift in voltage dependence; and IV) generation of an instantaneous current. The molecular basis for this classification was further interpreted using available cryo-EM structures of HCN1. Integration with clinical data from 50 patients revealed a striking correlation between functional class and clinical presentation. Loss-of-function variants prevailed among individuals with milder phenotypes or without epilepsy, with the latter distinctively clustering within the channel selectivity filter. In contrast, gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with DEE. Finally, we demonstrate that allosteric modulators, including peptides NB6 and TRIP8bnano and the small molecule J&J12e, effectively normalize channel function across three of the four classes in vitro. These findings establish a biophysical framework for interpreting HCN1 variants, demonstrating that the direction of channel dysfunction is a major determinant of epilepsy risk and severity, and providing a conceptual foundation for future class-based precision medicine approaches.

title: The TNKS/PI31-proteasome axis as a central node in TDP-43 neuropathies.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pathological aggregation of Tar DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) and disruption of neuronal protein homeostasis are defining features of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), and related TDP-43 proteinopathies. Efficient axonal transport of proteasomes is essential for maintaining local protein quality control in neurons. Proteasome inhibitor 31 (PI31) regulates both 26S proteasome assembly and dynein-mediated transport of 20S proteasomes. Although Tankyrase 1/2 (TNKS)-mediated ADP-ribosylation of PI31 promotes 26S proteasome assembly, its role in proteasome transport and its contribution to TDP-43 pathology remain unclear. METHODS: Live-cell imaging was performed to examine 20S proteasome transport in primary cortical and motor neurons from wild-type and Prp-TDP-43A315T transgenic mice. Protein interactions among TDP-43, TNKS, and PI31 were analyzed by immunoprecipitation and Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET). Insoluble protein accumulation and colocalization were assessed by RIPA/urea fractionation, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence. Proteasome assembly and activity were evaluated using native gel electrophoresis and a 20S proteasome-specific fluorogenic substrate. TDP-43 aggregation was examined by semi-denaturing detergent agarose gel electrophoresis (SDD-AGE). RESULTS: In cell models expressing TDP-43-FL, TDP-43-A315T, or TDP-25 and in Prp-TDP-43A315T transgenic mice, pathological TDP-43 species formed distinct aggregates, ranging from oligomers to prominent cytoplasmic aggregates, yet all reduced proteasome activity, impaired axonal proteasome transport, and caused the accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins, PI31, 20S proteasomes, and TDP-43 in the proximal axon and cell body. Pathological TDP-43 sequestered TNKS and proteasome components into insoluble fractions, thereby limiting the availability of free and soluble TNKS for interaction with PI31 and subsequent PI31 ADP-ribosylation, ultimately impairing 19S/20S proteasome assembly. Notably, disruption of the TNKS-PI31 interaction or inhibition of TNKS activity recapitulated the proteasome dysfunction induced by pathological TDP-43, supporting a role for the aberrant TNKS-TDP-43 interaction and consequent impairment of TNKS-mediated PI31 ADP-ribosylation in TNKS/PI31/proteasome axis dysfunction. CONCLUSIONS: Pathological TDP-43 disrupts proteasome function by impairing the TNKS/PI31/proteasome axis, suggesting that this axis may represent a potential therapeutic target for TDP-43 proteinopathies. Selectively restoring this pathway may enhance pathological TDP-43 clearance while minimizing nonspecific proteasome activation, thereby providing a more precise and safer therapeutic strategy for ALS and FTLD.

title: A homozygous C2ORF78 variant is associated with mTOR hyperactivation and neurodevelopmental defects in focal cortical dysplasia.
abstract: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a malformation of cortical brain development, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate type II FCD in a proband with behavioral disturbances, including aggression, hyperactivity, and sleep dysfunction, but with normal early development and cognition. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the proband revealed focal cortical thickening, abnormal sulcation, and gray-white matter blurring in the left temporal lobe, consistent with FCD type II. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous missense variant in C2ORF78 (c.1264 A > G; p.Ser422Gly), absent in population databases. The S422 residue is evolutionarily conserved, resides within a disordered, solvent-accessible region, and its substitution with glycine caused marked structural destabilization, cytosolic mislocalization, and protein aggregation. Functional studies in proband fibroblasts revealed no significant reduction of C2ORF78 protein, deregulated mTOR signaling, impaired autophagy, ER stress, and G0/G1 cell cycle arrest. Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed significant loss of protein stability and compactness in the S422G mutant. C2ORF78 interacts with RNA-binding and transcriptional regulators, and gene ontology analyses indicated roles in transcription and RNA splicing. We propose that C2ORF78 functions as a transcriptional coregulator of genes negatively regulating mTOR signaling. Mislocalization of the S422G mutant leads to a loss of nuclear function, resulting in hyperactivation of mTOR and disrupted cellular homeostasis. High expression of C2ORF78 in cerebral cortex and hippocampus supports its relevance to brain physiology. Our findings identify C2ORF78 as a novel candidate gene associated with FCD type II and highlight transcriptional dysregulation of mTOR signaling as a potential pathogenic mechanism.

overview: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a malformation of cortical brain development, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood.
main: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the proband revealed focal cortical thickening, abnormal sulcation, and gray-white matter blurring in the left temporal lobe, consistent with FCD type II.

title: Avocado Oil Nanoemulsion Ameliorates STZ-Induced Diabetic Brain Dysfunction through PI3K/AKT/mTOR-Related Gene Modulation and Attenuation of Apoptosis.
abstract: Diabetes mellitus is associated with progressive neurological complications characterized by hyperglycemia-induced oxidative stress, neuronal apoptosis, and disruption of intracellular survival signaling pathways. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of avocado cold-pressed oil (ACPO) and its nano-formulation against diabetes-induced cerebral alterations in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced diabetic rats. Seventy adult male Wistar rats were randomly allocated to ten groups (n = 7/group): normal control (NC), blank nano-formulation vehicle control (BC), metformin control (RC), ACPO control (OC), ACPO nano-formulation control (FC), diabetic positive control (PC), diabetic blank nano-formulation vehicle control (BT), diabetic + metformin (RT; 500 mg/kg), diabetic + ACPO (OT; 500 mg/kg), and diabetic + ACPO nano-formulation (FT; 500 mg/kg). The untreated diabetic group served as the reference for diabetes-associated alterations, whereas the diabetic vehicle-control group was included to account for potential effects of the nano-formulation vehicle. Diabetes was induced by a single intraperitoneal injection of STZ (40 mg/kg). Plasma glucose levels, cerebral gene expression of phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K), protein kinase B (AKT1), mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), pannexin-1 (PANX1), and acetylcholinesterase (AChE) were evaluated. Histopathological examination and caspase-3 immunohistochemistry were performed to assess neuronal injury and apoptosis. Treatment with ACPO and its nano-formulation significantly reduced plasma glucose levels and modulated key molecular pathways involved in neuronal survival. Both treatments upregulated PI3K, AKT1, and mTOR expression while downregulating GSK3β, PANX1, and AChE compared with untreated diabetic rats. Histopathological examination demonstrated marked preservation of cerebral cortical architecture, accompanied by reduced caspase-3 immunoexpression, indicating attenuation of neuronal apoptosis. The nano-formulation exerted greater effects on the investigated molecular biomarkers than conventional ACPO and produced histopathological and immunohistochemical improvements comparable to those observed with metformin.

title: AKT is necessary for neuronal hypertrophy and epilepsy caused by Pten knockout.
abstract: Phosphatase and tensin homologue on chromosome 10 (PTEN) is a key negative regulator of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway. Mutations in PTEN are highly implicated in autism spectrum disorder, epilepsy, congenital hydrocephaly and macrocephaly. While the conditional genetic knockout of Pten in murine neurons results in hypertrophy, increased migration, excitatory synaptogenesis, hyperexcitability and epileptiform activity, the specific downstream signalling mediators of these pathologies remain to be fully elucidated. Using retroviral-mediated genetic manipulation of individual neurons within the Cre-lox recombination system, we have analysed pathway outputs in response to the manipulation of various genes using immunohistochemistry, confocal microscopy and extensive morphological analyses, alongside whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology and 120-h video-EEG monitoring for seizure assessment. Here, we demonstrate that signalling through AKT is necessary for the development of neuronal overgrowth, increased excitatory synapse formation, excessive migration and hyperexcitability fuelled by the loss of PTEN function. Notably, the concurrent deletion of Akt1 and Akt3 isoforms was sufficient to effectively rescue hypertrophic neuronal morphology and physiology. These findings establish AKT as the essential mediator through which PTEN deficiency manifests, providing a transformative therapeutic target to correct the morphological and functional defects central to PTEN-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: HIV-1 Tat drives genotype-dependent neuroimmune programs that promote Parkinson Disease-like neurodegeneration in the hSNCAA53TGba1 mouse model.
abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type I (HIV-1) infection can induce both motor and cognitive impairments even in patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy (cART). These neurological alterations are related to direct and indirect mechanisms represented by viral and immune mediated processes, respectively. HIV-1 directly elicits neurological damages through some viral proteins including transactivator of transcription (Tat), a protein involved in the HIV-1 replication and able to affect neural cell through autocrine and paracrine pathways. In this study, we investigated the functional and transcriptional effects of intrastriatal Tat injection in pre-symptomatic mice carrying the hSNCAA53TGba1+/+ and hSNCAA53TGba1+/L444P mutations, common genetic risk factors for Parkinson's disease (PD). Behavioural assessment revealed that Tat administration anticipated motor symptoms onset in both genotypes, with some behavioural measures suggesting greater impairment in mice carrying both mutations, whereas spatial memory was not affected. In line with these findings, Tat injection induced significant loss of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive cells and fibre density in hSNCAA53TGba1+/L444P mice. HIV-1 Tat injection did not significantly modify TH-positive fibre density in hSNCAA53TGba1+/+ mice, whereas a marked reduction was observed in hSNCAA53TGba1+/L444P mice. Transcriptomic analysis revealed genotype-dependent responses, with a predominant innate immune-related signatures in hSNCAA53TGba1+/+ mice and transcriptional alterations involving immune, lysosomal, proteostatic, and autophagy-related pathways hSNCAA53TGba1+/L444P mice mice. Altogether, these findings indicate that HIV-1 Tat administration is associated with genotype-dependent PD-related motor deficits and that the Gba1 deficiency is linked to a more pronounced dopaminergic and transcriptional response to Tat exposure.

title: Crocin attenuates dopaminergic neuronal injury in 6-OHDA-induced PD rats: associations with mitochondrial protection and p38/p53 signaling.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the degeneration of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc). Crocin (CRO) has been reported to possess antioxidant and neuroprotective properties. However, whether its neuroprotective effects are associated with preserved mitochondrial integrity and alterations in p38/p53 signaling remains unclear. METHODS: A unilateral rat model of PD was established by stereotaxic injection of 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) into the right striatum. Rats were randomly assigned to four groups: control, 6-OHDA, 6-OHDA+CRO (30mg/kg), and 6-OHDA+levodopa (L-DOPA; 50mg/kg). Motor function was evaluated using the beam balance, rotarod, and cylinder tests. Nissl staining was performed to quantify neurons in the SNc, while tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) immunohistochemistry was used to assess DA neurons in the SNc and DA fibers in the striatum. Mitochondrial ultrastructure was examined using transmission electron microscopy(TEM), and mitochondrial function was assessed by measuring ATP content and mitochondrial complex I activity in substantia nigra (SN) tissue. Oxidative stress markers were measured in serum and tissues from the SN and striatum using commercial assay kits. Protein levels of TH, p53, total and phosphorylated p38, Bax, Bcl-2, and caspase-3 were determined by Western blotting. RESULTS: CRO treatment significantly ameliorated 6-OHDA-induced motor deficits (p < 0.01, p < 0.001, p < 0.0001) and attenuated reductions in TH-positive neuron counts in the SNc (p < 0.01) and striatal TH optical density (p < 0.01). TEM revealed that CRO alleviated mitochondrial ultrastructural damage and increased the mitochondrial aspect ratio (p < 0.001). These improvements were accompanied by increased ATP content (p < 0.01) and mitochondrial complex I activity (p < 0.05) in SN tissue. Furthermore, CRO increased CAT activity and GSH levels while reducing MDA levels in serum, SN, and striatum (p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 0.001), while SOD activity increased significantly in both brain regions (p < 0.0001). Western blot analysis showed that CRO increased TH protein expression (p < 0.01), reduced the p-p38/p38 (p < 0.05) and Bax/Bcl-2 (p < 0.05) ratios, and decreased p53 (p < 0.05) and caspase-3 (p < 0.01) protein levels compared with the 6-OHDA group. CONCLUSIONS: CRO attenuated motor deficits and nigrostriatal DA damage in a 6-OHDA-induced rat model of PD. These neuroprotective effects were associated with reduced oxidative stress, preserved mitochondrial morphology and function, and decreased p38 phosphorylation and p53 expression. These findings support further investigation of CRO as a potential neuroprotective compound for PD.

title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

title: Dinotefuran aggravates Alzheimer's disease-associated microglial inflammation through the CHUK/NFKB1-mediated NF-κB signaling pathway.
abstract: Neonicotinoid pesticides are widely used systemic insecticides with increasing evidence of neurotoxicity. However, their potential contribution to Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related neuroinflammation remains poorly understood. In this study, seven representative neonicotinoid pesticides were systematically evaluated by integrating physicochemical characterization, target prediction, pathway enrichment analysis, human AD snRNA-seq, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and experimental validation. Among the seven compounds, dinotefuran was prioritized based on its favorable blood-brain barrier permeability and enrichment in inflammation-related pathways. Integration of target prediction with AD transcriptomic analyses identified CHUK and NFKB1 as key candidate targets associated with NF-κB signaling. snRNA-seq analysis further demonstrated preferential enrichment of NF-κB signaling activity in microglia from AD brains. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations supported potential interactions between dinotefuran and IKKα (CHUK) as well as NF-κB1 (p50). In Aβ-treated BV2 microglia, dinotefuran further enhanced activation of the CHUK/NFKB1-mediated NF-κB signaling pathway, accompanied by increased expression of IKKα, phosphorylation of IκBα and p65, enhanced NF-κB1 activation, and elevated secretion of IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, IFN-α, and IFN-β. These pro-inflammatory effects were markedly attenuated by the NF-κB inhibitor BAY11-7082. Collectively, our findings suggest that CHUK/NFKB1-associated NF-κB signaling may contribute to dinotefuran-enhanced inflammatory responses in Aβ-treated BV2 microglia, providing preliminary mechanistic insights into the potential involvement of neonicotinoid pesticides in AD-related neuroinflammation.

title: Serum Aberrant Expression of Long Non-coding RNA LINC00365 and its Diagnostic Value in Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder. The present study aimed to elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying long non-coding RNA LINC00365 (LINC00365)-mediated regulation of AD pathogenesis.MethodsA total of 135 AD patients and 135 healthy controls were enrolled. The expression of LINC00365, microRNA-429 (miR-429), and F-box and WD repeat domain-containing 7 (FBXW7) was measured by real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). In vitro, AD cell models were established by treating SH-SY5Y neuronal cells and BV2 microglial cells with amyloid-β25-35 (Aβ25-35). Cell viability, apoptosis, and inflammatory cytokine levels were assessed using Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8), flow cytometry, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), respectively. Subcellular localization of LINC00365 was analyzed by nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation. The direct binding was validated by RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) and dual-luciferase assays.ResultsSerum LINC00365 was markedly decreased in AD patients with potential diagnostic value, and its level declined as dementia severity increased. In vitro, LINC00365 overexpression significantly ameliorated Aβ25-35-induced reductions in SH-SY5Y cell viability and apoptosis, and suppressed the release of tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) from BV2 microglia. Mechanistically, cytoplasmic-localized LINC00365 directly sponged miR-429, and FBXW7 was verified as its downstream target. Rescue experiments showed that miR-429 mimic reversed LINC00365-mediated FBXW7 upregulation and neuroprotection, whereas FBXW7 overexpression restored cell viability, attenuated apoptosis, and reduced inflammatory cytokine levels.ConclusionLINC00365 showed potential diagnostic value for AD in the present cohort. Mechanistically, it acted as a competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) to sponge miR-429, thus elevating FBXW7 and relieving Aβ25-35-triggered neuronal injury and neuroinflammation.

title: Computational modelling of acetylcholine deficiency-mediated dysfunction in the basal ganglia-thalamocortical network related to Parkinson's disease dementia.
abstract: Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) is a significant form of dementia. Its pathophysiology involves not only the dopaminergic system impairment but also the degeneration of cholinergic neurons in the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN), which is considered a potential contributor to the cognitive decline in PDD. Therefore, this study develops a computational model of the PPN-modulated basal ganglia-thalamic-cortical network to investigate how acetylcholine deficiency affects cortical oscillations. Based on anatomical evidence, acetylcholine deficiency is modeled by modulating synaptic connections from the PPN to the thalamus and basal ganglia output nuclei. Power spectrum analysis shows that acetylcholine deficiency, whether in the PPN-thalamic nucleus pathway or in the PPN-basal ganglia output nucleus pathway, leads to a decrease in cortical power ratio between the high-frequency band and low-frequency band. These results qualitatively reproduce the characteristics of electrophysiological measurements recorded in PDD. Further dynamical analysis suggests that this reduction may be associated with weakened oscillatory activity, reflected by a shift in neuronal firing patterns from limit cycle to point attractor. Moreover, simulations of combined acetylcholine and dopamine deficiencies reveal that both neurotransmitters can reduce the cortical power ratio, with a synergistic interaction rather than a simple additive effect. These findings provide a systems-level perspective on how ACh deficiency may contribute to cortical dysfunction in PDD and may offer a potential direction for future therapeutic research.

title: Comparative and combined neurotoxic effects of lithium carbonate and lead acetate in rats: From clinical alterations to molecular insights.
abstract: Heavy metal contamination in soil and water is a global concern with significant ecological and health implications. Lithium (Li), increasingly used in electric vehicles, and lead (Pb), a well-established pollutant, poses neurotoxic risks to animals and humans. This study evaluated the individual and combined effects of lithium carbonate (Li; 20 mg/kg) and lead acetate (Pb; 20 mg/kg) administered orally for 28 days in adult rats. Forty-eight rats were divided into four groups: control, Li, Pb, and Li + Pb. Clinical signs included hair loss, diarrhoea, dehydration, dullness, and foul-smelling faeces, with Li + Pb rats showing greater feed reduction and weight loss than single-exposure groups. Behavioural assessments revealed impaired motor coordination, anxiety-like behaviour, and significantly increased grip strength in Li + Pb as compared to the control group. Oxidative stress markers demonstrated significantly reduced Superoxide Dismutase (SOD), catalase, glutathione, and total antioxidant capacity, along with significantly elevated Malondialdehyde (MDA) and Nitric Oxide (NO) levels in the Li + Pb group compared with the control group. Brain AChE activity was significantly reduced in the Pb and Li + Pb groups compared with the control group. Gene expression analysis revealed significant downregulation of apoe (3.93-fold), app (6.15-fold), and ache (4.75-fold) genes, alongside bax (4.98-fold) upregulation in the Li + Pb group compared with the control group, indicating enhanced apoptosis, impaired antioxidant defense, and Alzheimer's-like neurodegeneration. Gross pathology revealed mild cerebral congestion in the Li and Pb alone groups, and marked congestion in the Li + Pb rats. Histopathology confirmed neuronal degeneration, Purkinje cell loss, perineuronal space widening, and astrocytic proliferation, with the Li + Pb group exhibiting the most severe lesions. Collectively, these findings suggest that co-exposure to lithium and lead exerts more pronounced neurotoxic effects, mediated by oxidative stress, apoptosis, and gene alterations linked to neurodegeneration.

title: Divergent tau pathology profiles induced by distinct alpha-synuclein aggregates in non-human primates.
abstract: Proteinopathies are frequently accompanied by co-pathologies, which complicate understanding the pathophysiological mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases. In this study, we employed a well-characterized baboon cohort to investigate the occurrence of tau pathology following intrastriatal injections of two distinct α-synuclein extracts [small aggregates (SA) and large aggregates (LA)] derived from the brains of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). Biochemical and histopathological analyses (6, 12 or 24 months after injections) revealed significantly higher phosphorylated tau expression and greater frequency of neuropil threads in both LA- (n = 18) and SA-injected baboons (n = 12) compared with control animals. We also observed distinct patterns of tau pathology depending on the assembly of α-synuclein aggregates. Baboons injected with SA exhibited tangle-like phosphorylated tau lesions and neuropil threads, with no significant differences across post-injection time points. Moreover, a uniform distribution of tau pathology was detected along the rostro-caudal axis of the medial temporal lobe, affecting neuronal, oligodendroglial and astrocytic cell types. On the other hand, baboons injected with LA exhibited neuropil threads and few glial lesions but lacked phosphorylated tau intraneuronal aggregates. The occurrence of phosphorylated tau lesions was associated with phosphorylated synuclein pathology. These observations suggest a link between nigrostriatal synucleinopathy and limbic tau co-pathology, providing pathophysiological insights into PD dementia.

title: Clinical and biochemical characterization of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in a CHCHD10 R15L family.
abstract: Familial forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are potential candidates for gene-directed therapies, but many recently identified genes remain poorly characterized. Here, we provide a comprehensive clinical, neuropathological and biochemical description of familial ALS (fALS) caused by the heterozygous p.R15L missense mutation in the gene CHCHD10. Using a cross-sectional study design, we evaluated five affected and nine unaffected individuals from a large seven-generation pedigree with at least 68 affected members. The pedigree suggests a high (68%-81%) but incomplete disease penetrance. Through cloning of the disease allele from distant members of the family, we establish the disease haplotype in the family. Notably, the haplotype was distinct from that of a previously reported p.R15L mutation carrier with ALS, demonstrating that the variant is in a mutational hotspot. The clinical presentation was notable for being highly stereotyped; all affected individuals presented with the rare ALS variant flail arm syndrome (FAS; also known as brachial amyotrophic diplegia or Vulpian-Bernhardt syndrome), suggesting greater involvement of the cervical spinal cord. Consistently, neuropathology from one family member demonstrated substantially increased CHCHD10 protein aggregation and neuronal loss (though absent TDP-43 pathology) in the cervical versus lumbar spinal cord. This FAS phenotype could be captured by a simple timed finger-tapping task, suggesting potential utility for this task as a clinical biomarker. Additionally, through analysis of fibroblast lines from 12 mutation carriers, isogenic induced pluripotent stem cells and a knock-in mouse model, we determined that CHCHD10 with the R15L variant is stably expressed and retains substantial function both in cultured cells and in vivo, in contrast to prior reports. Conversely, we find loss-of-function (LoF) variants are more common in the population but are not associated with a highly penetrant form of ALS in the UK Biobank (31 in controls; 0 in cases). Together, this argues against LoF and in favour of toxic gain-of-function as the mechanism of disease pathogenesis, similar to the myopathy-causing variants in CHCHD10 (p.G58R and p.S59L). Finally, through proteomic analysis of CSF of variant carriers, we identify that CHCHD10 protein levels are elevated approximately 4-fold in mutation carriers, and that affected and unaffected individuals are differentiated by elevation of two neurofilaments: neurofilament light chain (NfL) and peripherin (PRPH). Collectively, our findings help set the stage for gene-directed therapy for a devasting form of fALS, by establishing the likely disease mechanism and identifying clinical and fluid biomarkers for target engagement and treatment response.

title: The role of ZC3H14 (MSUT2) in neurodevelopment and tauopathies.
abstract: The processes of neurodevelopment and neuropathology can be influenced by RNA binding proteins. The RNA binding protein ZC3H14 (also referred to as MSUT2) is of particular interest for two reasons. First, homozygous loss-of-function alleles in ZC3H14 are associated with an inherited form of intellectual disability. Second, in model systems, loss of ZC3H14 can suppress the toxicity of tau aggregates, which are hallmark diagnostic features of Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative diseases referred to as 'tauopathies'. In this review, we discuss both the normal functions of ZC3H14 and how alterations in these functions may affect cognitive function or tau pathology. Although not fully understood, an emerging theme is that alterations in RNA regulation attributable to ZC3H14 loss can affect neuronal function.

title: Stalled Capillary Blood Flow in the Brain: New Measurement Tools Unveil a Critical Role in Neurological Diseases.
abstract: Flow disturbances in the smallest blood vessels of the brain, the capillaries, have long been considered a potential cause of brain dysfunction. However, owing to the technological challenge of studying blood flow in three-dimensional capillary networks, elucidating the incidence, causes, and consequences of capillary obstructions has been difficult. Advances in optical microscopes for in vivo imaging, primarily high-spatiotemporal-resolution optical coherence tomography and two-photon microscopy, have recently enabled detailed studies of these capillary stalling events in both healthy and diseased mice. In this review, we describe these imaging approaches to quantify capillary stalling, identifying strengths and weaknesses of different methods. We then review recent findings on the incidence, molecular and cellular causes, and physiological and neurological consequences of capillary stalling across multiple mouse models of brain disease, including Alzheimer's disease, stroke, and traumatic brain injury. We conclude by suggesting necessary next steps in instrumentation and analysis for studying capillary stalling, as well as how to address key unanswered questions about underlying mechanisms for capillary stalling in the brain and how this phenomenon may impact disease progression and cognitive function.

title: Intron Retention Caused by a Novel Homozygous LNPK Splice-Site Variant Leading to Severe Neurodevelopmental Disorder and Epilepsy.
abstract: Loss-of-function variants in LNPK have been shown to cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome associated with developmental delay, epilepsy, regression, and a distinct neuroimaging pattern including corpus callosum hypoplasia and abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity at the tip of the frontal horn of the lateral ventricles ("ear-of-the-lynx" sign). To date, 21 affected individuals from 16 families have been reported. Here, we identify a novel homozygous LNPK splice-site variant (NM_030650.3:c.27 + 1G>T) in a patient with developmental delay, severe intellectual disability, epilepsy, and a brain MRI demonstrating corpus callosum hypoplasia, "ear-of-the-lynx" sign, and substantia nigra signal alterations. To determine the variant's pathogenicity, we first used in silico splice prediction models AlphaGenome, SAI-10 k-calc, SpliceAI, and Pangolin. Then, by implementing targeted RNA sequencing of patient-derived fibroblasts following nonsense-mediated decay inhibition, we showed that the variant causes activation of a cryptic donor site, which results in a 5 bp intron retention and introduction of a premature stop codon into the transcript. We also delineate the phenotypic features of the proband with a comprehensive review of the literature. These findings expand the molecular spectrum of LNPK deficiency and demonstrate the complementary value of computational splicing prediction and functional RNA analysis for establishing the consequences of splice-site variants in rare-disease diagnostics.

title: Hagen-Poiseuille distributed-pressure model of osmotically-driven cytoplasmic flow in severed axons.
abstract: Repair (sealing) of traumatic plasmalemmal lesions involves the formation, movement, and accumulation of vesicles at the injury site by active transport and by passive bulk flow of cytoplasm. We show that hypotonic and hypertonic salines affect the direction and rate of vesicle movement in severed crayfish medial giant axons (CMGAs), presumably because osmotically-driven changes in intracellular pressure alter bulk cytoplasmic flow along the axon and at the lesion site. We develop a general Hagen-Poiseuille pressure-cable biophysical model of bulk cytoplasmic flow to predict direction and relative rate of cytoplasmic influx and efflux for CMGAs and other axons modeled as fluid-filled cylinders with distributed osmotic water permeability. Although our general-model applies to axons of any length, this model simplifies for a short-cable model in which the axonal length is much shorter than the hydraulic length constant, i.e., axons like CMGAs. Both General- and Shortcable-Models predict that hypotonic extracellular conditions drive transmembrane water flux into an axon, elevating intracellular pressure that is relieved by cytoplasmic efflux at the injury site. Conversely, hypertonic conditions drive transmembrane water flux out of the axon that is relieved by extracellular fluid influx at the severed end. Our data from CMGAs show that active transport involving molecular motors associated with microtubules and actin in CMGAs is the predominant contributor to vesicle movement towards severed end. Bulk cytoplasmic flow - as assessed by the movement of vesicles and cellular debris that persist when active transport is inhibited - is a lesser contribution to vesicle movement whose extent depends on the difference between extracellular and intracellular osmolarity. Our Hagen-Poiseuille distributed-pressure Model accurately predicts the direction and approximate rate of movement of vesicles and cellular debris under all osmotic conditions tested. Our Model should also account for vesicle behavior in other axons and cylindrical cytoplasmic processes of various diameters and lengths.

title: Mechanistic Study on Neurotoxicity Induced by Neodymium Oxide Exposure via TNT-Mediated Transfer of Damaged Mitochondria.
abstract: The health issues caused by the global mining, processing, and utilization of rare earth elements are receiving increasing attention. This study examined the molecular mechanisms mediating damaged mitochondria transfer via TNTs during neodymium oxide (Nd2O3)-induced neurotoxicity. Adult Sprague-Dawley rats were administered Nd2O3 by gavage, and effects on spatial learning and memory were assessed in the Morris water maze. Primary astrocytes and whole brain tissues from SD rats were extracted to identify differentially expressed genes via RNA-seq, and qRT-PCR and Western blotting were employed to perform targeted analyses of genes and proteins involved in blood-brain barrier (BBB) maintenance, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and mitochondrial dynamics. Alterations in calcium homeostasis, oxidative stress markers, and mitochondrial metabolism were measured using dedicated assay kits. TNT formation and mitochondrial migration were examined in co-cultures of primary astrocytes with HT22 neuronal cells by fluorescence staining under laser confocal microscopy. The stability of the F-actin-Myo19-Miro1 complex was evaluated using Co-IP and molecular docking, and the effects of Nd2O3 exposure on mitochondrial transport carriers and the number of TNTs were assessed. Finally, the role of TNTs in damaged mitochondria transfer was demonstrated by co-culturing astrocytes and neurons in a Transwell system and performing mitochondrial membrane potential detection. Neuronal damage was verified using TUNEL staining. Exposure to Nd2O3 caused dose-dependent spatial learning and memory impairment, reduced neural expression of core BBB genes, disrupted intracellular calcium homeostasis, induced oxidative stress, reduced OXPHOS, and promoted mitochondrial fragmentation. Astrocytes exposed to Nd2O3 formed TNTs with neurons, and damaged mitochondria were transported through TNTs containing the F-actin-Myo19-Miro1 complex, ultimately aggravating the degree of neuronal damage. We conclude that neodymium neurotoxicity involves mitochondrial oxidative stress and kinetic damage. Neodymium acts as a promoting factor through the F-actin-Myo19-Miro1 complex, transferring damaged mitochondria from astrocytes to neurons via TNTs and ultimately causing nerve damage.

title: Tubulin autoregulation mediator TTC5 regulates neuronal morphology and migration.
abstract: Microtubule dynamics are essential for neuronal development, yet how neurons regulate tubulin levels remains poorly understood. Tetratricopeptide repeat domain 5 (TTC5) mediates tubulin autoregulation, the co-translational degradation of tubulin transcripts in response to excess soluble tubulin, and TTC5 mutations cause cerebral atrophy with speech and motor impairment. Here, we show that tubulin autoregulation is active in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and depends on TTC5. TTC5 loss, or structure-guided mutations that disable autoregulation suppress microtubule polymerization, axonal outgrowth, and arborization, while enhancing cellular motility. Motility changes extend to non-neuronal cells, where they alter focal adhesion dynamics and can be rescued by manipulating soluble tubulin levels. Furthermore, downregulation of TTC5 interactor and autoregulation mediator S-phase cyclin A-associated protein in the endoplasmic reticulum (SCAPER) also suppresses neurite outgrowth and enhances motility. In vivo, TTC5 loss in mouse cortical projection neurons disrupts axon and dendrite arborization and causes hypermigration, recapitulating the cellular phenotypes observed in vitro. Patient-derived TTC5 disease mutants phenocopy this motility dysregulation, directly linking loss of TTC5 function to neurological deficits seen in patients. Together, these findings establish TTC5 as an essential regulator of neuronal morphogenesis and connectivity, with direct implications for TTC5-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

title: Tubulin autoregulation factors recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MTOCs for neuronal microtubule nucleation.
abstract: Neuronal function and survival depend on stereotyped non-centrosomal microtubule (MT) arrays. How these arrays form remains poorly understood. Here, we found that two factors previously implicated in tubulin mRNA turnover control neuronal MT content through γ-tubulin-dependent nucleation. In C. elegans neurons, loss of scaper, ttc5, or both reduced MT numbers to a similar degree as depletion of γ-tubulin, the main MT nucleator. Using conditional single-cell degradation alleles and endogenous tagging, we find that scaper and ttc5 are required to recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MT organizing centers (MTOCs). SCAPER is also instructive, as its overexpression raises γ-tubulin levels at nucleation sites and increases MT density. SCAPER, TTC5, and γ-tubulin are dispensable for developmental axon growth but play essential roles during regeneration, where SCAPER recruits γ-tubulin to a growth-cone-localized MTOC to orient MT nucleation. Last, SCAPER is required for activity-dependent MT nucleation in rat hippocampal neurons, suggesting a conserved role. These findings reveal mechanisms governing neuronal cytoskeleton assembly and function and suggest potential crosstalk between tubulin autoregulation and MT nucleation.

title: Redox-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial nucleoids contributes to bioenergetic decline during neuronal aging.
abstract: Why mitochondria progressively fail in aging neurons remains a fundamental question in neurobiology. Although bioenergetic decline and oxidative stress are hallmarks of aging, whether redox signaling remodels mitochondrial nucleoids (mt-nucleoids) to impair neuronal bioenergetics remains unclear. Using aged mouse neurons and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons, we demonstrate that redox-driven mt-nucleoid remodeling underlies reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and bioenergetic decline. Combining minimal photon fluxes (MINFLUX) nanoscopy with single-molecule transcription mapping, we identify distinct mt-nucleoid architectures governed by mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM)-mediated mtDNA compaction. Aging-associated oxidative stress drives mt-nucleoid remodeling from compact, transcriptionally active structures toward decompacted forms with reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and impaired mitochondrial ATP production. This remodeling involves species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms: cysteine oxidation promotes human TFAM polymerization, whereas methionine oxidation weakens mouse TFAM-mtDNA interactions. Notably, expressing an oxidation-resistant TFAM variant restores mt-nucleoid organization, mtDNA transcript abundance, and ATP production in aged neurons, identifying mt-nucleoid architecture as a potential target for preserving neuronal bioenergetics during aging.

title: Improved quality and reproducibility of cerebral cortical organoids under microfluidic culture conditions: a proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Cerebral organoids have emerged as advanced three-dimensionalin vitromodels capable of recapitulating essential aspects of human brain development, thereby offering new opportunities for studying brain physiology and disease. Nonetheless, their use in preclinical settings remains limited by their high variability. Microfluidic devices offer a promising alternative to conventional culture supports by enabling improved recapitulation of the cellular microenvironment; however, most cerebral organoids-on-chips rely on custom-made academic prototypes, limiting their scalability and translatability. Here, we established a standardized brain organoid-on-chip model by combining a regionalized cortical organoid differentiation protocol with a commercially available microfluidic device (Duplex™, NETRI). Cortical organoid quality and reproducibility were evaluated using a previously established multi-criteria Quality Control (QC) framework based on a scoring system. To enhance objectivity and throughput, the non-invasive morphometric QC criteria were automated using deep learning-based image analysis. Using a single human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) line, we assessed whether microfluidic culture conditions could improve the quality and reproducibility of cortical organoids within a controlled genetic background. Compared with conventional cultures, on-chip cortical organoids displayed improved inter- and intra-batch reproducibility across multiple scales, including morphology, size, cytoarchitectural organization, and transcript expression, together with higher QC scores and reduced QC failure rates. Finally, the QC framework was adapted for neurotoxicity assessment using a decision tree to classify compounds according to their neurotoxic risk. While this study represents a proof-of-concept demonstration within a single genetic background, the integrated brain organoid-on-chip platform and standardized QC evaluations provide a flexible and translatable approach for preclinical and industrial studies and support future validation across multiple hiPSC lines.

title: Region-resolved multi-layer proteomics reveals proteostasis-centered post-translational remodeling during mouse brain aging.
abstract: Brain aging is a spatially heterogeneous and multi-layered process, yet how protein abundance and post-translational modifications (PTMs) are coordinated across brain regions and over time remains incompletely understood. Here, we present a brain-region-resolved, multi-layer proteomics atlas of mouse brain aging, integrating the proteome, phosphoproteome, acetylome, and ubiquitinome across 11 anatomical regions and five time points spanning from young adulthood to senescence. Using dia-PASEF with PTM-optimized acquisition, we quantified 11,460 proteins with 29,225 phosphorylation sites, 5345 acetylation sites, and 5197 ubiquitination sites across 628 injections, enabling systematic analysis of age-associated molecular trajectories. We find that aging patterns are highly region-specific at both the protein and PTM levels, and the pons emerges as a region with marked phosphorylation-level alterations in aging-related signaling pathways. Notably, we uncover a proteostasis-centered regulatory axis in the aging hippocampus, where reduced ubiquitination and increased acetylation converge on Tau, potentially impairing its degradation. Using a telomerase-deficient mouse model (Tert KO), we show that telomere dysfunction perturbs aging-associated molecular trajectories and induces a divergent proteostasis and stress-response state distinct from physiological brain aging. Together, our study provides a spatiotemporal multi-layer proteomics resource of brain aging and reveals a proteostasis-centered landscape of post-translational remodeling associated with region-specific vulnerability and Tau dysregulation.

title: Inflammatory signature of subcutaneous fat after weight loss and regain in women undergoing repeated bariatric surgery.
abstract: CONTEXT: Repeated metabolic-bariatric surgery (MBS, r-BS) represents 10-25% of all MBS and is commonly-performed for weight regain after prior significant weight-loss. It remains unclear how adipose tissue adapts to surgically-induced weight-loss-regain in obesity. OBJECTIVE: We hypothesized that compared to primary bariatric surgery (p-BS), women undergoing r-BS exhibit a distinct adipose tissue signature. DESIGN: Subcutaneous/visceral adipose tissues (SAT/VAT, respectively) from female MBS patients were assessed histologically/molecularly/functionally (activation of human microglia cells by SAT-secretome). SETTING: Elective MBS in a public university hospital. PATIENTS: Women undergoing either p-BS, or r-BS with documented >15% weight-loss after prior MBS. INTERVENTION: MBS. MAIN OUTCOME MEASUREMENT: Inflammation in SAT. RESULTS: Women undergoing r-BS (n=21) trended to be older than those undergoing p-BS (n=35)(47.2 vs. 40.5y, p=0.06), with a lower BMI (42.3 vs. 45.6 kg/m2, respectively, p=0.103), and a trend for improved cardiometabolic risk parameters (fasting insulin, CRP and HDL-c). Adipocyte size, adipose tissue fibrosis, macrophage and crown-like structures abundance were similar, while mast-cells were slightly more prevalent in r-BS. Single-nucleus RNA-seq-based deconvolution algorithm applied unto bulk RNA-seq confirmed the absence of a major shift in adipose tissue cell-type composition. Yet, RNA-seq revealed unique transcriptome of r-BS SAT, with activation of inflammatory pathways. Consistently, SAT explants from r-BS secreted higher protein concentrations of NFκB-regulated cytokines IL6/IL8. Functional impact of the more inflammatory-secretome was suggested by its increased ability to inflammatory-activate human microglia cells. CONCLUSIONS: Prior BS-induced weight-loss and subsequent regain in women is associated with inflammatory transcriptome and secretome of SAT that can activate cultured human microglia cells.

title: Decoding cell division history and lineage-resolved phenotypic patterns from single-cell barcode and transcriptomic data.
abstract: The cell division tree encodes how proliferation and differentiation generate cellular diversity during multicellular development. Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing and CRISPR-based lineage tracing have enabled retrospective reconstruction of these histories at single-cell resolution. Here, we present FateScape, a statistical framework that integrates paired lineage barcodes and transcriptomic profiles to infer cell division topology and characterize depth-resolved phenotypic patterns. FateScape combines barcode consistency with transcriptome-derived state continuity through overlapping state-lineage decomposition and barcode-guided subtree integration. Here, to analyze phenotypic patterns on the inferred tree, we introduce entropy paths, which measure how cells of each state are distributed across depth-defined subtrees, and Moran's I-derived statistics for same-state autocorrelation and cross-state association. In simulations, FateScape shows robust reconstruction performance across varying mutation rates, dropout levels, sample sizes, and barcode target-site numbers. In the Caenorhabditis elegans data analysis, FateScape accurately recovers lineage topology and identifies depth-resolved state patterns, including concentrated intestinal cells and broadly distributed neuronal and glial states. In mouse embryos, FateScape quantifies distinct germ-layer patterns, including early endodermal concentration, broad ectodermal distribution across shallow-to-intermediate depths, and intermediate mesodermal distribution followed by deeper concentration. Together, FateScape provides a framework for reconstructing cell division histories and quantifying state dispersion, concentration, and tree-based association across lineage depth.

title: Subcellular compartment determines signal dominance: Endosomal cAMP overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation from a single receptor.
abstract: Cells convey information not only via the identity of activated signaling pathways but also through the subcellular location where those signals originate. Whether spatially distinct signals from a single activated receptor compete to determine net cellular output has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate this principle for a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), showing that endosomal and plasma membrane signals from a single activated receptor are not merely distinct but functionally opposed, with endosomal signaling predominating to reverse the net cellular output. Using the adhesion GPCR GPR64/ADGRG2 as a model system, we show that ligand activation engages two spatially distinct G-protein pathways that are not just additive but functionally opposed: plasma membrane G13/RhoA activation and Gs/cAMP production that persists from endosomes following receptor internalization. The endosomal cAMP pool actively overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation, resulting in net RhoA inactivation, an outcome that is completely reversed by pharmacological blockade of endocytosis or endosomal Gs inactivation. In parathyroid cells, where GPR64 is highly expressed, this endosomal signal dominance suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion independently of extracellular Ca2+ levels. These findings support a model in which the subcellular compartment, rather than pathway identity, determines the dominant signal and the overall cellular response of a single activated receptor, with implications for understanding the complexity of GPCR signaling.
