title: Tian Wang Bu Xin Dan Attenuates Neuronal Injury in LPS-Treated HT22 Cells and PCPA-Induced Insomnia-Model Rats.
abstract: Tian Wang Bu Xin Dan (TWBXD) is traditionally used for sleep disorders, but its neuroprotective mechanisms remain unclear. This study evaluated a cinnabar-free modified TWBXD preparation in cellular and animal models, focusing on phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT) expression, autophagy-related markers, inflammation, and apoptosis. An aqueous TWBXD extract was profiled by untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Candidate compounds annotated by LC-MS and checked against PubChem records were used for target prediction, followed by intersection with insomnia-related genes, protein-protein interaction analysis, and functional enrichment. TWBXD-containing serum was evaluated in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-treated HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells. Rapamycin and 3-methyladenine were used to probe autophagy-related processes. In p-chlorophenylalanine (PCPA)-treated rats, pentobarbital-induced sleep responses, locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, spatial learning and memory, and hippocampal CA1 pathology were assessed. Twenty high-confidence candidate compounds yielded 553 predicted human targets, of which 144 overlapped with insomnia-related genes. Network analysis identified 10 candidate hub genes, including AKT1, MTOR, BCL2, TNF, and IL6, and highlighted PI3K-Akt, autophagy, apoptosis, and inflammatory pathways. In LPS-treated cells, rapamycin shifted several autophagy-related and inflammatory markers toward control levels. TWBXD-containing serum increased Beclin 1 expression and the microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3-II to light chain 3-I (LC3-II/LC3-I) ratio, decreased p62, interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), Bax, and caspase 3, and increased interleukin-10 (IL-10) and Bcl-2. PI3K and AKT protein and messenger RNA (mRNA) levels also shifted toward control levels. Several TWBXD-associated molecular changes were attenuated by 3-methyladenine. In PCPA-treated rats, TWBXD improved pentobarbital-induced sleep responses, anxiety-like behavior, and spatial learning and memory and alleviated hippocampal CA1 neuronal injury. These findings support the neuroprotective effects of cinnabar-free modified TWBXD in the models examined. Behavioral and histological improvements were accompanied by changes in PI3K/AKT expression and autophagy-, inflammation-, and apoptosis-related markers.

title: STING-dependent TNF signalling promotes IKKβ-mediated ATG9A phosphorylation and autophagy.
abstract: Chemotherapeutic drugs, either alone or in combination with immunotherapy, are routinely used in cancer treatment. However, cancer cells frequently develop resistance to chemotherapy, and the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using head and neck squamous cell carcinoma as a model, we show that chemotherapy activates the cGAS-STING pathway, leading to the induction of TNF. TNF mediates a paracrine signalling pathway in recipient tumour cells, leading to IKKβ activation and ATG9A phosphorylation at serine 654, thereby promoting autophagy. Moreover, IKKβ activation and ATG9A S654 phosphorylation are induced by TNF, nutrient deprivation and mTOR inhibition, suggesting that the IKKβ-ATG9A axis may represent a common regulatory mechanism of autophagy. Analysis of patient samples further reveals that chemotherapy induces autophagy, and elevated phosphorylation of ATG9A at S654 correlates with poor chemotherapy response. Of note, TNF blockade enhances therapeutic efficacy in both chemotherapy alone and chemotherapy combined with immune checkpoint inhibition. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized TNF-IKKβ-ATG9A signalling axis that promotes autophagy and highlight TNF blockade as a promising strategy to overcome chemotherapy resistance.

title: Hepatocyte-derived exosomal miR-122 mediates liver-to-brain crosstalk and neuroinflammation in alcohol-exposed Alzheimer's disease mice.
abstract: Neuroinflammation and microglial activation are common features in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and excessive alcohol consumption. Alcohol induces liver damage and inflammation, and altered serum aminotransferases have been reported in patients with AD. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) and their cargo are emerging as mediators of intercellular communication in AD and alcohol-induced liver injury. However, the effects of alcohol use on AD progression remain to be elucidated. In this study, we evaluated the effects of repeated binge drinking on the liver and brain in the APP/PS1 mouse model of AD. Alcohol-exposed APP/PS1 mice showed elevated serum alanine aminotransferase levels, indicating liver injury absent in controls, along with increased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in both liver and brain. Alcohol increased the biogenesis and release of sEVs in AD mice and in mouse hepatocytes. These sEVs were enriched in mature miR-122-5p that is predominant in hepatocytes. In vivo, miR-122-5p was detected in the brain of alcohol-exposed AD mice suggesting EV-mediated miR-122-5p transfer to the brain. Microglial uptake of hepatocyte-derived sEVs was confirmed in vitro. sEVs from alcohol-treated hepatocytes sensitized BV-2 microglia to LPS stimulation, significantly enhancing CCL2, CXCL2, CCL3, and TNF-α production. Transfection of microglia with a miR-122-5p mimic partially recapitulated the pro-inflammatory sensitization by sEVs from alcohol-exposed hepatocytes, which was reversed by miR-122-5p inhibitor delivery. ADAM10, a miR-122-5p target, was reduced in both wild-type and AD brains after alcohol exposure, with cell-specific effects. These results suggest that alcohol-induced hepatocyte-derived sEVs may modulate liver-to-brain signaling via miR-122-5p and contribute to neuroinflammation in AD.

title: The Red Nucleus in Motor Control and Autism Spectrum Disorder.
abstract: Neuromotor differences of motor coordination, timing, postural regulation, and prospective motor control are common and emerge early in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, their underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood, with existing research emphasising cortical and cerebellar systems. This review re-examines the red nucleus (RN), a midbrain structure embedded within cortical, cerebellar, and olivary motor pathways, as an underexplored component of distributed sensorimotor networks. We synthesise evidence from comparative neuroanatomy, animal experiments, human neuroimaging, movement disorders, and autism research, distinguishing direct RN findings from broader circuit-level inferences. Neuroimaging studies have reported RN-region susceptibility differences in autistic children, including an exploratory association with fine-motor development, but reproducible links to specific motor processes and RN-related causal mechanisms remain unestablished. We therefore propose a testable hypothesis that differences in RN structure, function, or connectivity may be associated with specific dimensions of motor function in autism. Error-related sensorimotor adaptation provides a primary experimental target, complemented by prospective motor control. Future investigations combining RN-sensitive neuroimaging, quantitative motor assessment, and transdiagnostic comparisons with developmental coordination disorder may determine whether RN-related measures provide explanatory information beyond sensorimotor systems. This framework positions the RN as a candidate component of autism-related motor networks.

title: Isolation and lipidomic profiling of neuronal lipid droplets to unveil the lipid landscape of neurodegenerative disorders.
abstract: Recent advances have expanded the role of lipid droplets (LDs) beyond passive lipid storage, implicating their involvement in various metabolic processes across mammalian tissues. Neuronal LDs, whose existence has long been debated, have now been identified in several neural structures, raising questions about their contribution to neurodegenerative disorders. Elucidating the specific chemical makeup of these organelles within neurons is critical for understanding their role in neural pathologies. However, the inherent submicron size and low abundance in neurons have posed challenges in their isolation and physical and biochemical characterization. Here, we present our Protocol that overcomes this obstacle: we blocked neuron-specific triglyceride lipase to enlarge LDs, rendering them amenable to flotation in a sucrose gradient. We further used an improved methodology of lipidomic analysis on the LDs purified from cultured primary neurons, offering insights into their unique lipid composition. This Protocol can be implemented by researchers with basic expertise in neuronal culture, imaging, ultracentrifuge handling and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry analysis. The complete workflow requires 3-4 weeks, from neuronal culture to lipidomics analysis. Future integration of this method with high-throughput techniques holds promise for uncovering disease-specific alterations in lipid metabolism, providing new avenues for potential therapeutic interventions.

title: Methods for Identification and Structural Characterization of Tau Polymorphs in Neurodegenerative Disease.
abstract: Tauopathies are neurodegenerative diseases associated with the misfolding and aggregation of the tau protein in the brain, including Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE). Current medical technology is only able to definitively diagnose tauopathies post-mortem, which limits patient treatment options and reduces quality of life. Structural differences related to specific tauopathies ultimately result in unique disease progression and require unique treatments. In particular, CTE-related tauopathies are relatively understudied compared to AD. To improve diagnosis and treatment options for patients with CTE, it is essential to understand the role of tau in disease onset and progression. Experimental methods such as atomic force microscopy (AFM) and computational methods such as molecular dynamics simulations have been used to gain an understanding of pathological tau structure and mechanics. Spectroscopy and molecular probes have also been effective in revealing mechanisms of tau aggregation. State-of-the-art methods such as cryogenic electron microscopy and two-dimensional infrared spectroscopy (2DIR) are now being used to further explore tau at atomic resolution. In this review, we discuss the current state of both experimental and computational strategies in the assessment of tauopathies, specifically related to structural characterization. We highlight technological advances in relevant methods, such as AFM and 2DIR, that are pivotal to our understanding of structural amyloid formation and progression ante-mortem.

title: From internal discrimination to external transportability: A multi-layer evaluation of gestational maternal-blood transcriptomic signals associated with later neurodevelopment.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Maternal blood transcriptomic profiles during pregnancy may capture biological states associated with later neurodevelopment, but internally detectable signals may not transport across populations, tissues, molecular layers, or experimental systems. We evaluated the internal robustness and cross-context transportability of a pathway-level maternal gestational transcriptomic signal associated with later atypical neurodevelopment. METHODS: Maternal gestational blood transcriptomes from 214 MARBLES pregnancies were summarized using 619 prespecified pathway scores and modeled for atypical versus typical neurodevelopment using repeated nested cross-validation. Internal signal specificity was assessed by repeating the complete discovery procedure after 1000 outcome-label permutations. The resulting pathway findings were then evaluated across independent transcriptomic cohorts, orthogonal methylomic datasets, autism common-variant genetic data, developmental brain atlases, and CRISPR perturbation of neurodevelopmental-risk genes in human neural cells. RESULTS: The discovery procedure achieved an out-of-fold ROC-AUC of 0.693, PR-AUC of 0.677, and Brier score of 0.227, outperforming all 1000 phenotype-permuted runs of the same pipeline (empirical P = 0.001). Leave-one-batch-out performance was heterogeneous. Independent cord-blood transcriptomics provided limited directional support, whereas placental transcriptomics did not replicate the signal. Methylomic analyses showed limited support, common-variant genetics showed no detectable convergence, and neural CRISPR perturbations showed no functional convergence. Developmental atlas analysis demonstrated strong localization of the fetal inhibitory-interneuron pathway to inhibitory neurons. CONCLUSIONS: The maternal gestational blood signal was internally distinguishable from chance expectations but showed limited transportability across independent biological contexts. These findings distinguish within-cohort molecular predictiveness from broader biological generalizability and support multi-context stress testing before prenatal molecular signals are interpreted as portable biomarkers or mechanisms.

title: Early milestones and neurodevelopment in children with mitochondrial disease.
abstract: AIM: To quantify neurodevelopmental functioning in children with primary mitochondrial disease (MtD), and to assess relationships with other clinical data. METHOD: This study was performed as a cross-sectional analysis of a longitudinal cohort. Inclusion criteria were age over 12 months, genetically confirmed MtD. Clinical data were obtained by caregiver interview and medical records abstraction. Measures included IQ, Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition, the International Pediatric Mitochondrial Disease Scale (IPMDS), and Gross Motor Functional Classification System (GMFCS) level. An exploratory approach analyzed the relationship between clinical data and other measures, using Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition as a dependent variable. RESULTS: The cohort included 32 children, mean age 7 years (SD = 3 years 6 months). The most common genotypes included MT-ATP6 (n = 6) and the mitochondrial aminoacyl tRNA synthetase family of genes. Regarding phenotype, 15 out of 32 (47%) met clinical criteria for Leigh syndrome. Clinical descriptors of disability included 18 out of 32 (56%) with intellectual disability/global developmental delay; 13 out of 32 (40%) were non-ambulatory and 6 out of 32 (19%) reported developmental regression, primarily in the motor domain. The mean Full Scale IQ was 54 (SD = 27) and adaptive behavior composite (ABC) standard score was 66 (SD = 20) with motor subscale lower than other domains. The ABC was negatively associated with IPMDS, GMFCS, and seizures. Of those who walked and talked by 24 months and had neuroimaging with zero or one brain region affected (n = 9), eight (89%) had adaptive function in the average range. INTERPRETATION: Children with MtD exhibit a wide range of neurodevelopmental function. Overall MtD adaptive function was low, with motor-predominant disability, and correlated negatively with other measures of severity. Episodic developmental regression occurred in a minority of this cohort but primarily affected motor skills.

title: SARS-CoV-2 mRNA Vaccination in Pregnancy and Child Neurodevelopment at 18 to 30 Months.
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Little is known about neurodevelopmental outcomes of children exposed to SARS-CoV-2 messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccine during pregnancy. Evidence on long-term offspring outcomes after in utero exposure to SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination is needed to inform vaccine recommendations in pregnancy. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether there is an association between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or shortly before pregnancy and offspring neurodevelopmental measures. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This multicenter, prospective, cohort study of 18- to 30-month-old children was conducted at 14 centers of the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units Network from 2024 through 2025. Women who received a SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine during or within 30 days prior to pregnancy (exposed) were matched with women who did not (unexposed) by delivery site, delivery date, insurance status, and race and ethnicity. These data were analyzed from June 2025 to May 2026. EXPOSURES: Maternal receipt of at least 1 dose of an mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccine during, or within 30 days prior to, the index pregnancy vs no SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during pregnancy or within 30 days prior. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was Ages and Stages Questionnaire version 3 (ASQ-3) total score, which was deemed to be equivalent between the exposed and unexposed groups if the 90% CI of the median difference was between -10 and 10. Secondary outcomes included domain-specific ASQ-3 scores, the Child Behavior Checklist, Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, and Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire scores. RESULTS: Of 3956 screened, 271 exposed and 240 unexposed children were enrolled. Matching on all characteristics was possible in 217 pairs. Of the 434 children enrolled, 258 (59.4%) were Non-Hispanic White, 96 (22.1%) Non-Hispanic Black, 52 (12.0%) Hispanic, and 28 (6.5%) were not represented by any of the above racial or ethnic groups. Median age at assessment was 25.8 [24.6 to 28.3] months, 221 were female (50.9%), and 213 were male (49.1%). Exposed mothers were more likely to be nulliparous; their children were slightly younger at assessment and more likely to have been vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2. The primary outcome of ASQ-3 score was equivalent between the exposed and unexposed groups (255 vs 260, adjusted median difference, -3.4; 90% CI, -9.8 to 3.0). There were no significant differences in secondary outcomes. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this multicenter cohort study, ASQ-3 scores were equivalent between 18- to 30-month-old children whose mothers did or did not receive mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or immediately prior to pregnancy. These findings support continued recommendations for SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination during pregnancy.

title: A rare TMEM175 mutation drives Parkinson's disease pathology by disrupting proton gating and lysosomal acidification.
abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175), implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, has been variably proposed to function as a background K+ "leak" channel or a proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Here, we identified the rare TMEM175 variant p.L275R in a patient with early onset PD. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that TMEM175-L275R mutant proteins retain normal lysosomal expression and K+ "leak" activity, but specifically lose proton- and agonist-dependent activation gating. In skin fibroblasts isolated from the patient with PD harboring the monoallelic p.L275R mutation (TMEM175+/L275R), and in derived induced pluripotent stem cells and induced dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal H+ flux, acidification, and degradation were impaired. These lysosomal defects were corrected upon genome editing to produce the isogenic WT allele (+/+Cor), but appeared when the mutant allele was introduced onto a WT background (+/L275RMut). Pathological α-synuclein aggregation was facilitated in patient-derived (+/L275R) and mutation-introduced (+/L275RMut) neurons. Consistent with these genetic findings, pharmacological activation of TMEM175 with small-molecule agonists restored lysosomal functions and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in TMEM175+/L275R neurons. In in-vivo studies, equivalent-site-mutation knock-in mice demonstrated synucleinopathy and PD-like motor phenotypes. Collectively, our work provides genetic and pharmacological evidence that severe loss-of-function mutations may contribute causally to the onset age and pathogenesis of PD and identifies lysosomal proton channels and transporters as potential therapeutic targets for PD intervention.

title: SSH1 knockdown increases autophagosome formation through ATG9A recruitment and promotes MAPT/tau protein degradation.
abstract: Pathological accumulation of MAPT/tau protein is a defining feature of Alzheimer disease (AD) and related tauopathies, highlighting the need to identify druggable regulators of MAPT/tau clearance. Using Drosophila behavioral assays focused on cytoskeletal remodeling pathways dysregulated in AD, we identified genes whose genetic modulation mitigates MAPT/tau-induced behavioral deficits. These modifiers were validated by histopathology and mechanistically examined in human tauopathy cell models to determine their impact on autophagy-dependent MAPT/tau degradation. Autophagic flux, ATG9A trafficking, and autophagosome biogenesis were further analyzed. Across models, reduction of the phosphatase SSH1 consistently lowered steady-state MAPT/tau levels by enhancing autophagic flux through a mechanism distinct from its canonical regulation of CFL1. Mechanistically, SSH1 functions as a negative regulator of early autophagosome formation: SSH1 depletion promotes ATG9A mobilization to the endoplasmic reticulum-phagophore assembly site (ER-PAS), thereby accelerating autophagic vesicle biogenesis. Importantly, the MAPT/tau-lowering effect of Dmssh attenuation was abolished in flies haploinsufficient for DmAtg9, demonstrating that SSH1-mediated MAPT/tau clearance requires ATG9 function. Consistent with a direct regulatory interaction, in vitro phosphatase assays revealed that recombinant SSH1 decreases ATG9A phosphorylation in the presence of actin, identifying an SSH1-ATG9A regulatory axis controlling autophagosome initiation. These findings position SSH1 as a nodal inhibitor of autophagy initiation whose inhibition enhances MAPT/tau proteolysis. Notably, SSH1 haploinsufficiency also reduces SNCA/α-synuclein accumulation in vivo, indicating broader relevance to neurodegenerative proteopathies. By integrating in vivo functional screening with mechanistic studies in human cells, this work identifies SSH1 as a druggable phosphatase that constrains autophagy at the level of ATG9A-dependent vesicle formation.Abbreviations: Aβ: amyloid-beta; AD: Alzheimer disease;AMP-AD: Accelerating Medicines Partnership-Alzheimer's Disease; ANOVA: analysis of variance;ATG9A: autophagy related 9A; BDSC: Bloomington Drosophila stock center; BSA: bovine serum albumin; CFL1: cofilin 1; DIOPT: DRSC Integrative Ortholog Prediction Tool; DmAtg9: Drosophila ortholog of ATG9; DMEM: Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium; DMSO: dimethyl sulfoxide; Dmssh: Drosophila ortholog of SSH1; Dmtsr: Drosophila ortholog of CFL1 and CFL2; ER-PAS: endoplasmic reticulum-phagophore assembly site; ESCRT: endosomal sorting complexes required for transport FC: fold change; FTD: frontotemporal dementia; HeLa: Henrietta Lacks; LIMK: lim domain kinase; MTOR: mechanistic target of rapamycin kinase; ND: neurodegenerative disease; NFE2L2/Nrf2: nuclear factor, erythroid derived 2, like 2; PBS: phosphate-buffered saline PD: Parkinson disease; PFA: paraformaldehyde; PHF-1: paired helical filament 1; RNAi: RNA interference; ROSMAP: The Religious Orders Study and Memory and Aging Project; SDS-PAGE: sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis; snRNA-seq: single nucleus RNA-sequencing; SQSTM1/p62: sequestosome 1; SS inhibitor: SAR405 + SBI-0206965 inhibitors; SSH1: slingshot protein phosphatase 1; ULK1: unc-51 like kinase 1; WT: wild type.

title: The Path to Kinesin and Beyond.
abstract: The recognition that the components of the axon and synapse originated in the neuronal cell body and were transported to their final destinations was recognized as early as Ramon y Cajal's pioneering studies on regeneration. However, mechanisms by which this transport was accomplished remained a mystery even as information accumulated about the rates and the composition of material being transported. The challenge was a lack of knowledge about molecular motors. In the early 1980's, advances in live cell imaging in combination with a novel model for study of vesicle transport in the axon led to the discovery of a new family of molecular motors, the kinesins.

title: Plasma P-Tau217 and NfL Longitudinal Changes Across Neurodegenerative Diseases: Impact of α-Synuclein in Alzheimer Disease.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Plasma phospho-tau217 (p-tau 217) is a validated biomarker of Alzheimer disease (AD), and its longitudinal dynamics may reflect AD progression. Plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) reflects axonal injury and neurodegeneration. Their trajectories may be modulated by concomitant proteinopathies such as α-synuclein (aSyn). We aimed to characterize longitudinal changes (36 months) in plasma p-tau217 and NfL across neurodegenerative and non-neurodegenerative cognitive disorders and to examine biomarker trajectories according to aSyn pathology status within AD. METHODS: In this prospective single-center cohort, participants were recruited from a memory clinic in Barcelona, Spain. Participants were eligible if they had cognitive impairment because of neurodegenerative or non-neurodegenerative conditions between 2019 and 2022 and if baseline and 3-year follow-up blood samples were available. CSF AD biomarkers measured with Lumipulse and aSyn pathology assessed using real-time quaking-induced conversion assay were determined at baseline and used for patient diagnosis. Plasma p-tau217 and NfL were measured with Lumipulse at baseline and 36 months and analyzed as study outcomes. Between-group differences at longitudinal level were assessed using linear mixed-effects models. RESULTS: A total of 223 participants were included: 92 AD-aSyn- (69.6 [5.6] years, 57.8% female), 15 AD-aSyn+ (69.1 [5.8] years, 53.3% female), 17 dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)-AD- (70.9 [6.8] years, 23.5% female), 13 DLB-AD+ (age 72.3 [5.0] years, 30.8% female), 48 frontotemporal lobar dementia (FTD) (65.5 [8.8] years, 45.8% female), and 38 non-neurodegenerative cognitive impairment (NNCI) (65.3 [7.7] years, 35.9% female). At baseline, AD-aSyn+ and AD-aSyn- groups showed the highest plasma p-tau217, whereas DLB-AD+ showed intermediate levels and DLB-AD-, FTD, and NNCI the lowest. Over 36 months, AD-aSyn+ exhibited the steepest increase in p-tau217 (2.19 pg/mL; p < 0.001), whereas AD-aSyn- and DLB-AD+ showed smaller increases; DLB-AD-, FTD, and NNCI remained stable. For NfL, FTD and AD-aSyn+ had the highest levels at baseline and follow-up (both p < 0.001), with similar increases. AD-aSyn-, DLB-AD+, and DLB-AD- showed intermediate values with moderate increases, whereas NNCI displayed limited changes. DISCUSSION: Plasma p-tau217 changes longitudinally in AD, and its trajectory is modulated by α-synuclein pathology. Patients with AD-aSyn+ show higher levels of NfL, similar to FTD, highlighting greater neuroaxonal injury. α-synuclein positivity identifies an AD-aSyn+ subgroup with steeper increases in p-tau217 and NfL, supporting biomarker-based stratification for prognosis and trial enrichment.

title: IGF signaling in autism and related neurodevelopmental disorders: Biomarkers and therapeutic targets.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD), including both idiopathic and syndromic forms, is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired social communication, restricted and repetitive behaviors, and diverse molecular etiologies. Increasing evidence implicates dysregulation of insulin-like growth factor (IGF) signaling in ASD and related neurodevelopmental disorders, including Rett syndrome, Angelman syndrome, Fragile X syndrome, Phelan-McDermid syndrome, and schizophrenia. However, the diagnostic and therapeutic significance of IGF1 and IGF2 across these disorders remains incompletely understood. This review synthesizes recent evidence on the roles of IGF1 and IGF2 as biomarkers and therapeutic targets in syndromic and idiopathic ASD and related neurodevelopmental disorders. Preclinical and clinical evidence suggests that dysregulated IGF signaling contributes to disease pathogenesis by altering the PI3K/AKT/mTOR and MAPK/ERK pathways, which regulate neuronal survival, neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity and cognitive function. IGF1 exhibits the strongest clinical evidence, particularly in Rett syndrome and Phelan-McDermid syndrome, whereas IGF2 shows promising therapeutic potential for improving learning, memory, and synaptic function in Angelman syndrome, Fragile X syndrome, and schizophrenia. Metformin studies also demonstrate effects on metabolic and behavioral outcomes through pathways overlapping with IGF signaling, although direct IGF1 or IGF2 mediation remains unestablished. Clinical translation remains limited by small study populations, methodological heterogeneity, inconsistent biomarker findings, and insufficient long-term safety data. This review highlights IGF signaling disorders and emphasizes its potential for biomarker development, targeted therapeutics, and precision medicine. Future multicenter clinical trials integrating multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence, and standardized biomarker validation will be essential to translate IGF-based interventions into clinical practice.

title: Proteomics and synaptome mapping to uncover diversity in excitatory synapses.
abstract: Synapses are the fundamental computational units of the brain. Although synapses are classically classified according to the neurotransmitter they use, glutamatergic excitatory synapses also exhibit marked heterogeneity in their molecular composition and structure. Understanding this diversity requires comprehensive approaches that go beyond small-scale, candidate-based analyses of synapses. Proteomic analyses of biochemically enriched synaptic fractions have provided unbiased, quantitative measurements of synaptic protein composition, revealing differences across brain regions, cell types, developmental stages, and physiological and pathological states. Proteomics has also revealed the composition and remodeling of synaptic protein complexes, as well as changes in post-translational modifications. In parallel, synaptome mapping, an imaging-based approach for the large-scale in situ analysis of synapses across the brain, has emerged as a form of spatial omics. In this approach, synapses labeled with a small set of synaptic proteins are systematically imaged across the brain. Synaptome mapping reveals whole-brain variation in synapse molecular identity and structural features, including differences in synapse size, shape, and spatial distribution in vivo. Together, these approaches show that excitatory synapses are diversified across anatomical, cellular, developmental, activity-dependent, and disease-related contexts. These complementary perspectives will advance our understanding of the synaptic mechanisms underlying neural computation, behavior, and brain disorders.

title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity.
abstract: Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive "sleeping" nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

title: A Cilia-Centered Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD+) Signaling Network Regulates Hypothalamic Lysosomal Homeostasis and Metabolic Aging.
abstract: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an essential metabolite that regulates diverse cellular metabolic processes. Primary cilia, hair-like organelles on the cell surface, function as critical signaling hubs. Here, we demonstrate that cellular NAD+ levels are key regulators of both primary cilia growth and lysosomal function in hypothalamic neurons. NAD+ depletion induces ciliary shortening and diminishes lysosomal activity in a cilia-dependent manner. Mechanistically, the lysosomal repair complex protein CHMP4B translocates from periciliary satellites to lysosomes during lysosomal stress, a process impaired by ciliary dysgenesis. Disrupted lysosomal recruitment of CHMP4B leads to abnormal lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and lysosomal dysfunction. Aged mice with hypothalamic NAD+ deficiency exhibit shortened cilia and lysosomal stress phenotypes, both of which are restored by calorie restriction (CR). Moreover, CR improves aging-associated metabolic dysfunction, at least in part, through hypothalamic cilia-dependent mechanisms. These findings identify a primary cilium-mediated-NAD+ signaling axis that maintains lysosomal homeostasis in hypothalamic neurons, the disruption of which drives metabolic aging.

title: FOXJ1 transcriptional targets in human airway cells and impaired multiciliogenesis in FOXJ1-associated primary ciliary dyskinesia.
abstract: Fluid mobilization on epithelia is ensured by the motile cilia of differentiated multiciliated cells (MCCs). Key transcriptional regulators of motile ciliogenesis include CCNO, MCIDAS, RFXs, and the transcription factor FOXJ1, whose precise role in humans remains unclear. We show that, unlike CCNO and MCIDAS, FOXJ1 expression persists in well-differentiated human airway epithelial cells (hAECs), suggesting functions beyond cilia initiation. Chromatin-immunoprecipitation sequencing in human airway epithelial cells allowed us to refine the consensus target motifs of FOXJ1 and RFXs, as well as their close proximity, which strongly suggests functional cooperation within a transcriptional complex. By combining chromatin-immunoprecipitation sequencing in normal cells with RNAseq from patients with FOXJ1-related primary ciliary dyskinesia, we identified 683 direct FOXJ1 target genes. Among these, 89 MCC-enriched genes-particularly those encoding axonemal proteins such as microtubule-inner proteins and dynein arm docking components-were downregulated in FOXJ1-deficient cells. Collectively, these findings provide new insights into how FOXJ1 contributes to human motile ciliogenesis and reveal a potential role for FOXJ1 in maintaining MCCs differentiation and ciliary function by sustaining the expression of ciliary proteins, particularly those in direct contact with axonemal tubulin.

title: Intranuclear localisation of KLF3-AS1 under the balance of histone acetylation and methylation in BMSCs ameliorates cerebral ischaemia‒reperfusion injury by preserving microglial mitochondrial function and inhibiting inflammatory polarisation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ischaemic stroke occurs when blood flow to the brain is obstructed. Rapid restoration of blood supply frequently induces cerebral ischaemia‒reperfusion injury (CIRI). Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC)-derived exosomes exhibit promising therapeutic potential for CIRI. In-depth exploration of their therapeutic mechanisms holds crucial significance for CIRI management. METHODS: The middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO) model was established in mice. An in vitro ischaemic stroke model was established by treating BV-2 cells with oxygen‒glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R). Exosomes were isolated from BMSCs and intranasally administrated into mice or added into BV-2 cells. Neurological deficits, grasping and coordination function were evaluated. Cell viability, apoptosis, proliferation and migration were examined. The localisation of KLF3-AS1 was examined by combined staining of immunofluorescence and fluorescence in situ hybridisation. Intracellular Ca2+ and adenosine triphosphate levels, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and membrane potential were assessed. RESULTS: KLF3-AS1 enhanced BMSC viability, proliferation and migration, accompanied by epigenetic reprogramming at its promoter characterised by increased H3K27 acetylation (H3K27Ac) and decreased H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27Me3). BMSC-derived KLF3-AS1-enriched exosomes indicated therapeutic efficacy in both in vivo and in vitro models of cerebral ischaemia. In MCAO-induced mice, these exosomes alleviated neurological deficits and shifted microglial polarisation from pro-inflammatory M1-like to anti-inflammatory M2-like phenotypes. Similar effects were observed in OGD/R-treated BV-2 microglia, where KLF3-AS1-enriched exosomes attenuated oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction while upregulating Silent Information Regulator 3 (SIRT3) expression. Mechanistically, KLF3-AS1 facilitated ETS Variant Transcription Factor 4 (ETV4) nuclear translocation to activate SIRT3 transcription in microglia, and inhibition of SIRT3 abolished the neuroprotective effects of exosomal KLF3-AS1. CONCLUSION: BMSC-derived exosomes delivering KLF3-AS1 ameliorates CIRI by preserving microglial mitochondrial function and inhibiting inflammatory polarisation, highlighting KLF3-AS1 as a critical epigenetic regulator and exosome-mediated therapeutic agent for CIRI through the ETV4/SIRT3 axis. KEY POINTS/HIGHLIGHTS: KLF3-AS1 enhances bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) function via promoter H3K27Ac/H3K27Me3 reprogramming. KLF3‑AS1 directly binds ETS Variant Transcription Factor 4 (ETV4) to activate Silent Information Regulator 3 (SIRT3), preserving mitochondrial integrity. BMSC‑derived exosomal KLF3‑AS1 promotes M2 microglial polarisation and ameliorates cerebral ischaemia-reperfusion injury.

title: Novel NaV1.6-Mitochondrial Complexes in Retinal Astrocyte Pockets Sequester GABA.
abstract: Voltage-gated sodium channels are best known for their capacity to generate and propagate electrical currents in neurons and muscle. Their expression in glial cells may also be of great importance given these cells' involvement in various disease processes. Here we identify a previously unrecognized voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.6-enriched microdomain in mouse retinal astrocytes. Using super-resolution confocal microscopy, electrophysiology, and transcriptomic analyses, we show that NaV1.6 forms high-density clusters within intracellular compartments devoid of the calcium-binding protein, S100β, typically understood to distribute throughout the entire astrocyte. These NaV1.6 pockets are polarized, clustering only on the bilayer facing retinal ganglion cell neurons, and are packed with unusually large, anaplerotic, and relatively depolarized mitochondria that closely appose NaV1.6 puncta. These metabolic compartments also accumulate high levels of GABA. Together, our findings reveal a specialized NaV1.6-mitochondrial complex in retinal astrocytes that expands the functional repertoire of voltage-gated sodium channels beyond direct neuronal electrical excitability.

title: STMN2: Membrane-Binding Microtubule Regulator or Tubulin Effector?
abstract: STMN2, a protein implicated in motor neuron degeneration, is widely viewed as a membrane-associated microtubule inhibitor, but emerging evidence challenges whether this activity defined its cellular function. Three alternative models integrates available evidence to offer perspectives beyond microtubule regulation. The vesicle cargo adaptor model proposes that STMN2 recruits diverse cargos to transport vesicles for axonal delivery. The membrane-bound signaling messenger model links STMN2 turnover to local signaling, effector, degradation, or effector release. The traffic director model proposes that STMN2 regulates cargo routing between delivery and degradative pathways. These models are not mutually exclusive and position tubulin binding as a regulator of STMN2 function rather than its defining activity.

title: Exosomes in Traumatic Brain Injury: From Secondary Injury Mechanisms to Cell-Free Neurorepair.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and long-term neurological disability worldwide. Exosomes (EXOs) have attracted increasing attention because they mediate intercellular communication and show promise as diagnostic biomarkers and cell-free therapeutics. However, the overall research landscape and evolving priorities of exosomes studies in TBI remain insufficiently characterized. METHODS: We performed a bibliometric analysis of publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus (search date: October 24, 2025) using equivalent search strategies combining traumatic brain injury and exosome/extracellular vesicle terms. English-language original research and review articles published between January 1, 2012 and October 24, 2025 were eligible; editorials, letters, conference abstracts, and non-English publications were excluded. After deduplication and screening, 609 publications were retained. A multi-tool analytical framework was employed: CiteSpace (v6.4.R1) for citation-burst detection, co-occurrence clustering, and timeline visualization; VOSviewer (v1.6.18) for collaboration network mapping and keyword co-occurrence analysis; and the Bibliometrix R package (v4.4.3) for descriptive statistics, productivity indicators (h-index, g-index, m-index), and performance metrics. RESULTS: From 2012 to 2025, research on exosomes in TBI expanded steadily, with accelerated growth after 2017. Keyword co-occurrence, citation-burst detection, and reference co-citation analyses showed a clear thematic evolution. Early studies and highly co-cited references primarily addressed secondary-injury mechanisms, particularly neuroinflammation, microglial activation, glial-neuronal interactions, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction. Influential work by frequently co-cited authors (e.g., Chopp M and Zhang Y) helped establish exosomes-mediated neuroprotection and neurovascular remodeling as central themes. More recently, burst keywords and emerging co-citation clusters have shifted toward mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes, cell-free therapeutic strategies, engineered exosomes, drug delivery systems, and regenerative medicine, reflecting a transition from mechanistic exploration to translational application. This shift has coincided with the growing prominence of journals such as the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, Journal of Neurotrauma, Cells, and Neural Regeneration Research as major publication venues for the field. CONCLUSION: This study maps the global landscape of exosomes research in TBI and traces its evolution from pathogenesis to regenerative therapy. The United States and China stand out as complementary leaders, with American groups focusing on mechanisms and biomarkers and Chinese groups driving therapeutic translation. Future priorities for clinical translation include standardized isolation protocols, optimal dosing regimens, and rigorous clinical trials. Together, these findings offer a practical framework to guide the development of exosome-based therapies for TBI.

title: Reduced BNIP1 impairs autophagosome-lysosome fusion in hippocampal neurons and contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathology.
abstract: BNIP1 (BCL2‑interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N‑ethylmaleimide‑sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that BNIP1 is a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP‑overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells, screened key interacting proteins of BNIP1 via mass spectrometry, and further performed gain‑ and loss‑of‑function assays using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNA (siRNA) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that, in these experimental models, reduced BNIP1 expression contributes to AD‑related pathological alterations by impairing autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b‑mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. This study suggests that reduced BNIP1 expression is involved in AD‑related pathological alterations.NIP1 (BCL2-interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, which renders BNIP1 a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP-overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells. Mass-spectrometry analysis was performed to screen key interacting proteins of BNIP1. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were further conducted using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that decreased BNIP1 may act as an important contributing factor mediating AD-associated autophagosome-lysosome fusion defects in these experimental models. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b-mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates aberrant autophagosome-lysosome fusion. This study suggests that BNIP1 serves as a potentially key regulatory protein for mechanistic research into Alzheimer's disease.

title: Lipid Droplet-Associated Hsp70 Palmitoylation Drives Lysosomal Dysfunction in Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: Lipid droplet (LDs) accumulate in glial cells across neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathologies. LDs modulate cellular stress via organelle crosstalk, particularly with lysosomes, whose dysfunction and cathepsin leakage drive glial activation after cerebral ischemia. However, the molecular link between accumulated LDs and lysosomes in pathological glial activation remains incompletely understood. Using a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) model and oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/Re) cell models, we found that both LD signal intensity and lysosomal cathepsin B leakage progressively increased from day 1 to day 14 after I/R. Etomoxir, an inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 A (CPT1A), the rate-limiting enzyme for fatty acid β-oxidation, aggravated I/R-induced LD accumulation and lysosomal damage in glial cells. Exogenous LDs derived from OGD/Re-treated glial cells aggravated lysosomal damage and promoted the proliferation of astrocytes and microglia. LD accumulation was associated with Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution of Hsp70 from lysosomes to the extracellular space, leading to lysosomal damage and reactive glial activation. Mechanistically, using multiple genetic and pharmacological approaches, including Plin3 knockdown, an Hsp70 palmitoylation‑site mutant, recombinant human Hsp70 (rhHsp70), as well as a pan-palmitoylation inhibitor and TLR2/4 antagonist, we consistently validated that Plin3, an LD surface protein, interacts with lysosomal Hsp70, causing Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, and lysosomal damage. Extracellular Hsp70 activates TLR2/4 on glial cells, promoting cell proliferation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release. Collectively, these findings indicate that pathological LDs interacting with lysosomes drive Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, causing lysosomal impairment and astrogliosis in ischemic stroke. We uncover Hsp70 palmitoylation as a potential drug target for ischemic stroke therapy.

title: Protein Quality Control Systems in Neurodegeneration-Chaperones, Cytoskeleton, and the Pathogenic Transition of Tau.
abstract: Maintenance of protein homeostasis is essential for neuronal survival, and its disruption is a defining feature of neurodegenerative diseases. Neurons are particularly vulnerable to proteostatic stress due to their post-mitotic nature, long lifespan, and dependence on cytoskeletal integrity for structural stability, intracellular transport, and synaptic function. In tauopathies and related neurodegenerative disorders, misfolded proteins and aggregation-prone proteins burden the cellular quality-control systems, leading to cytoskeletal destabilization, synaptic dysfunction, and progressive neuronal loss. This review is organized around a central question: for a given tau species, defined by its isoform, post-translational modifications, and assembly state, what determines its fate? We examine how molecular chaperone networks, including HSP100, HSP90, HSP70, J-domain proteins (JDPs), small heat shock proteins (sHSPs), and the Prefoldin-CCT pathway, regulate the folding, disaggregation, sequestration, and degradation of pathogenic tau. We highlight how these chaperone networks influence key proteostasis checkpoints, determine whether tau refolds, is degraded, or is redirected toward toxic aggregation, and how these outcomes impact microtubule stability and neuronal function. Drawing on studies in yeast, Drosophila, mammalian models, and human tissues, we develop two key conclusions. First, chaperone activity is not uniformly protective against tauopathies; its effects depend on the tau species, cellular context, and disease stage. Second, because the cytoskeleton is both a chaperone client and an essential component of intracellular clearance pathways, tau pathology and proteostasis failure can reinforce one another. Finally, we discuss emerging therapeutic strategies and challenges in targeting chaperone networks to restore proteostasis while avoiding unintended neurotoxic consequences.

title: TUBA1A mutations in cerebral cortical dysplasia.
abstract: The cerebral cortex is essential for higher cognitive functions, and its structural and functional integrity relies on the precise regulation of microtubule proteins in neuronal proliferation, differentiation, axonal and dendritic growth, migration, and connectivity. The TUBA1A gene, encoding alpha-tubulin, is highly expressed during fetal brain development and is crucial for cortical maturation. Research has linked mutations in the TUBA1A gene to malformations of cortical development (MCDs), but the specific types of MCDs caused by these mutations and the underlying molecular mechanisms are not fully understood. This review compiles current research findings on the development of the cerebral cortex, the role of microtubules in cortical development, and existing studies on the TUBA1A gene. It aims to elucidate how TUBA1A regulates microtubules to influence brain development, providing key insights into the gene's role in neural development.

title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons.
abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.

title: Evaluation of deep learning-based super-resolution reconstruction in fetal brain T2-weighted single-shot fast spin-echo imaging.
abstract: PURPOSE: The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of a deep learning-based Precise IQ Engine (PIQE) in enhancing image sharpness and quality during MRI reconstruction to enhance the image quality of fetal brain single-shot fast spin-echo (SSFSE) imaging. METHODS: Fetal brain MRI scans of 14 patients, including an SSFSE sequence, acquired between January 2024 and February 2025, were analyzed. Images were reconstructed with and without PIQE (zoom ratio of 3 from low-resolution matrices). We quantified the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and image sharpness using the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the fetal brain. Two board-certified radiologists assessed the image noise, contrast, sharpness, artifacts, and overall image quality of the two image types on a 4-point scale. We compared the quantitative and qualitative scores between the images with and without PIQE using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. RESULTS: SNRs, CNRs, and FWHM were significantly enhanced with PIQE compared to those without PIQE (SNR, CNR: p < 0.001, FWHM : p < 0.01). Qualitative scores for noise (p < 0.001), contrast (p < 0.001), sharpness (p < 0.001), artifacts (p < 0.001), and overall image quality (p < 0.001) were superior in images obtained with PIQE compared to those without it. Kappa analysis revealed moderate-to- excellent agreement for different image quality aspects: noise (κ = 0.52), contrast (κ = 0.74), sharpness (κ = 0.82), artifacts (κ = 0.61), and overall image quality (κ = 0.80). CONCLUSION: PIQE potentially enhances the image quality of fetal brain MRI using an SSFSE sequence.

title: Kinesin-12 (Kif15) in Neurons: From Mitotic Motor to Activity-Dependent Regulator of Dendritic Spines.
abstract: Kinesin-12 (Kif15) is a canonical mitotic kinesin that crosslinks parallel microtubules and suppresses microtubule catastrophe. It exists in both dimeric and tetrameric oligomerization states that are regulated by ionic conditions and binding partners. Its persistent expression in postmitotic neurons indicates that this ancestral microtubule-organizing activity has been repurposed for neuronal functions, yet the dendritic role of Kif15 has remained poorly defined. Here, we review and hypothesize KIF15 acting as a dendritic regulator. We propose that in the dendritic shaft, Kif15 exists predominantly as a tetramer crosslinker to organize the mixed-polarity antiparallel microtubule array. At the neck of the dendritic spines, perhaps due to the electrical signals, the compartmental ion concentration has changed. The dimeric Kif15 transports PSD95 along microtubule plus ends that invade dendritic spines and unloads PSD95 at the postsynaptic sites. There, synaptic activity triggers Ca2+ influx and CaMKII activation to promote Kif15 association with Myosin IIb (Myh10), forming a Kif15-Myh10 hetero-complex, which reorganizes the microtubule-actin network to facilitate mushroom-like dendritic spine formation. This framework explains why Kif15 loss impairs spine complexity, synaptic development, and mood-related behaviors without causing catastrophic disassembly of dendritic microtubules. It further links KIF15 mutations to cognitive disorders and suggests that mechanistic insights from a mitotic motor to its synaptic functions.

title: Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis ameliorates autistic behavior in a rat model of autism via cholinergic modulation in the prefrontal cortex.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: In the present study, we investigated whether deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis (NBM) improves autism spectrum disorder (ASD)-related behavioral abnormalities in a valproic acid (VPA)-induced rat model of autism, consistent with changes in cholinergic markers in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). METHODS: On the 12.5th day of gestation, pregnant rats ( n  = 16) received a single intraperitoneal injection of 500 mg/kg sodium valproate dissolved in 0.9% saline, while others ( n  = 5) received saline alone. Male offspring were allowed to reach 3 months of age and then were randomly assigned to one of four experimental groups: Contr - prenatally saline injected, VPA - prenatally VPA-injected, VPA/I - VPA-injected with electrode implantation in the NBM, and VPA/S - VPA-injected with electrical stimulation. DBS was initiated in rats of the VPA/S group 10 days after surgery (two consecutive hours per day, every day for 2 weeks; DBS parameters: 60 Hz, 120 µs, and 50 µA). RESULTS: The prenatally VPA-exposed rats demonstrate deficits in social behavior, increased locomotor activity, and reduced anxiety levels. Immunohistochemical evaluation shows a decrease in the number of acetylcholinesterase-immunoreactive neurons in the mPFC and choline acetyltransferase-immunoreactive neurons in the NBM. NBM-DBS improves VPA-induced autistic behavior and increases the number of acetylcholinesterase-immunoreactive neurons in the PFC. CONCLUSION: The correlation between ASD-like behavior and cholinergic markers in the mPFC supports our hypothesis that NBM-DBS improves behavioral deficits by modulating cholinergic neurotransmission in the PFC in a rat model of autism.

title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain.
abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal. Here we demonstrate a three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and nonlinear limits for safe laser exposure while satisfying the spatiotemporal requirements of single-cell resolution calcium (Ca2+) imaging. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

title: DINOSim: Training-Free Semantic Segmentation on Microscopy Images.
abstract: We present DINOSim, a training-free method for segmenting objects in microscopy images without the need for large annotated datasets or additional model training. DINOSim builds on the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder, which captures semantic information from images. By comparing the encoder's features of image patches to those of a user-selected reference, DINOSim generates pseudo-labels that guide semantic segmentation. Subsequently, a k-nearest neighbors framework is used to refine predictions across new images. Our experiments show that DINOSim can effectively segment previously unseen objects in diverse microscopy datasets, offering performance comparable to supervised approaches while avoiding the need for costly manual labeling. We also investigate how different choices of user prompt selection and model size affect accuracy and generalization. To make the method widely accessible, we provide an open-source napari plugin (github.com/AAitorG/napari-DINOSim), enabling researchers to apply DINOSim to their own data easily. Overall, DINOSim offers a fast, flexible and practical solution for bioimage analysis, particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings.

title: The pathological roles of intrinsically disordered proteins in lysosomal acidification dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and Parkinson's disease (PD) are characterized by the accumulation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), including amyloid-β (Aβ), tau, and α-synuclein (αSyn). These proteins disrupt neuronal homeostasis through toxic aggregation, impaired proteostasis, and progressive neurodegeneration, in part via dysfunction of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP). A central feature of this impairment is defective vacuolar-type (H+)-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, leading to lysosomal deacidification and reduced degradative capacity. Pathological IDP species converge on V-ATPase through direct interactions with its subunits or by perturbing its assembly, while also exerting protein-specific effects, including lysosomal membrane destabilization, impaired hydrolase activity, and disrupted endolysosomal trafficking. These combined mechanisms create a reciprocal relationship between lysosomal dysfunction and IDP accumulation, in which impaired lysosomal degradation further promotes the persistence and aggregation of pathological IDP species. This review synthesizes current insights into the molecular interplay between IDPs and lysosomal acidification across AD, FTD, and PD, and highlights how these processes contribute to disease progression. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring lysosomal function. These findings underscore lysosomal dysfunction as a common feature of IDP-driven neurodegeneration and a potential therapeutic target across these disorders.

title: Comprehensive Clinical, Neuroradiologic, and Oral Health of 23 Individuals With MOPDII: Molecular Spectrum and Phenotypic Features.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II (MOPDII; MIM #210720) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe growth failure and microcephaly, frequently complicated by central nervous system (CNS) anomalies and early-onset cerebrovascular disease. This study aimed to define the neurologic, radiologic, molecular, and oral-dental features of a MOPDII cohort, with particular emphasis on cerebrovascular involvement, and to assess genotype-phenotype correlations. METHODS: Molecular diagnosis was established using next-generation sequencing, including targeted gene panel sequencing (n = 11) and exome sequencing (n = 1), or Sanger sequencing (n = 11). Clinical data, neuroimaging and vascular findings, systematic oral-dental examinations, and molecular results were retrospectively reviewed. RESULTS: Twenty-three patients from 18 unrelated consanguineous families were included. Seventeen distinct homozygous PCNT variants were identified, including 5 splice-site, 5 frameshift, and 7 nonsense variants; of these, 12 were novel. Structural CNS anomalies were common, with the thin corpus callosum being the most frequent finding, observed in 14 of 17 patients (82%) who underwent cranial imaging. Moyamoya disease was identified in 12 patients (70.5%), of whom 7 experienced chronic or acute cerebral infarctions and/or intracranial hemorrhage. Three patients with moyamoya disease died of complications related to vascular involvement. The 2 oldest patients developed severe peripheral arterial and coronary artery occlusions, leading to spontaneous limb amputation and acute myocardial infarction. Oral-dental evaluation, performed in 14 patients (61%), revealed microdontia, malformed teeth, and root shortening. No consistent genotype-phenotype correlation was identified for cerebrovascular or orodental manifestations. DISCUSSION: MOPDII is strongly associated with moyamoya disease and represents a major cause of neurologic morbidity and mortality. Early and longitudinal neuroimaging, including brain MRI and angiographic assessment, should be integral to patient management. Oral-dental abnormalities are common and merit routine evaluation.

title: Alzheimer's genetic risk factor CASS4 controls microglial focal adhesion biology and amyloidosis.
abstract: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified numerous Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk genes enriched in microglia, including Crk-associated substrate (Cas) scaffold protein family member 4 (CASS4), which encodes the adaptor protein CASS4. Despite its strong genetic association with AD, the role of CASS4 in disease remains poorly understood. Here, we show that full-body Cass4 deletion in 5xFAD mice increases amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, neuronal dystrophy, and cognitive deficits. Since microglia are the predominant brain-resident cells expressing Cass4, we investigated its role in microglial responses to Aβ pathology. Loss of CASS4 impaired microglial mobilization to Aβ plaques and reduced plaque compaction. Phosphoproteomic analysis of purified microglia revealed marked disruption of focal adhesion signaling following Cass4 deletion. Consistent with this, CASS4 deficiency abrogated in vivo microglial recruitment to injury and in vitro wound healing responses, two processes that are centrally orchestrated by focal adhesion biology. Together, these findings identify CASS4 as a critical regulator of microglial function and focal adhesion biology and suggest that CASS4 may represent a therapeutic target for AD.

title: Non-electrophilic TRPA1 modulator MNP-021 protects neuronal and glial function from diabetes-associated glucotoxicity and neuroinflammation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Diabetes-associated neurodegeneration is amplified by methylglyoxal (MGO)-driven dicarbonyl stress linking hyperglycemia to neuronal insulin resistance and maladaptive neuroinflammation. We tested the neuroprotective activity of MNP-021, a non-electrophilic transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) modulator, in neurons and glial cells in vitro. METHODS: SH-SY5Y neurons were pretreated with MNP-021 and challenged with MGO, then profiled by high-content imaging, RNA-seq, Seahorse Oxygen Consumption Rate (OCR) and Extracellular Acidification Rate (ECAR), glycolytic stress assays, and immunoblotting for AKT, ERK, and cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB). In an additional sustained glucotoxicity paradigm, differentiated SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to high glucose for 7 days and viability was assessed by LIVE/DEAD™ high-content imaging. HMC3 glial cells were treated with MNP-021, exposed to Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), Tumor Necrosis Factor-α (TNF-α) or Aβ(25-35), and tested for viability and inflammatory markers by Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) and RT-qPCR. RESULTS: MGO increased nucleus-to-cytoplasm area ratio by 49% and dysregulated glucose handling, increasing 2-(N-(7-Nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-4-yl)Amino)-2-Deoxyglucose (2-NBDG) uptake by ~ 25%, with GLUT1/GLUT4 membrane redistribution; MNP-021 normalized morphology, glucose uptake, and transporter localization without cytotoxicity up to 10 µM. RNA-seq identified 754 MGO-deregulated genes, including ISR/metabolic nodes such as glucokinase (GCK), Sestrin-2 (SESN2), phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), Phosphoserine Aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1), phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 2 (PCK2); MNP-021 buffered stress-induced transcription with limited baseline effects, modulated mitochondrial morphology and redox-associated fluorescence while preserving overall respiratory flux and blunting stress-evoked compensatory glycolysis. MNP-021 restored pro-survival signaling (pAKT/pERK and nuclear pCREB), including insulin responsiveness during MGO exposure. In a sustained high-glucose model, MNP-021 reduced the high-glucose-associated increase in cell death, extending its protective effects beyond the acute MGO paradigm. MNP-021 reduced Interleukine-6 (IL-6)/TNF-α release while increasing Interleukine-10 (IL-10) and Arginase 1 (ARG1) (~ 1.9-fold vs. LPS/TNF-α) in HMC3 glial cells, shifting them toward a pro-resolving IL-10/ARG1 program with reduced amyloid β-peptide 25-35 (Aβ(25-35))-evoked cytokine release and Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) remaining very low (≤ 10 pg/mL) and not significantly increased in this system. CONCLUSIONS: MNP-021 coordinates transcriptomic restraint, transporter-level glucose handling, mitochondrial resilience, and pro-survival/pro-resolving signaling in neuron-microglia cell models. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of MNP-021 in dicarbonyl-linked neuro-metabolic stress and provide pharmacological evidence consistent with a TRPA1-linked component of its activity.
authors: De Carli A, Filipponi C, Polini B, Sancho-Bornez V, Basso E, Filippini F, Dardano A, Sardelli F, Daniele S, Contestabile M
overview: BACKGROUND: Diabetes-associated neurodegeneration is amplified by methylglyoxal (MGO)-driven dicarbonyl stress linking hyperglycemia to neuronal insulin resistance and maladaptive neuroinflammation.
main: RESULTS: MGO increased nucleus-to-cytoplasm area ratio by 49% and dysregulated glucose handling, increasing 2-(N-(7-Nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-4-yl)Amino)-2-Deoxyglucose (2-NBDG) uptake by ~ 25%, with GLUT1/GLUT4 membrane redistribution; MNP-021 normalized morphology, glucose uptake, and transporter localization without cytotoxicity up to 10 µM.

title: hucMSC-derived exosomes rescue cognitive impairment and Alzheimer-like pathology in APP/PS1 mice via metabolic remodeling.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation, with the latter as a central pathological hub. hucMSC-derived exosomes (hucMSC-exosomes) show therapeutic potential for AD, but their metabolic remodeling mechanisms remain unclear. We combined behavioral tests, pathological assays and untargeted metabolomics to investigate the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of hucMSC-exosomes in APP/PS1 AD mice. Seven-month-old male APP/PS1 mice were randomly divided into AD-vehicle and AD-hucMSC-exosome groups, with age-matched C57BL/6 mice as wild-type controls. All mice received tail vein injections for 6 weeks. Morris Water Maze tests revealed that hucMSC-exosomes significantly improved spatial learning and memory in AD mice. Pathological analyses confirmed that hucMSC-exosomes reduced cerebral Aβ deposition, suppressed hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and restored antioxidant capacity (SOD, GPx, GSH/GSSG). Untargeted metabolomic analysis of brain tissues revealed that 6 primary carbon, 8 primary nitrogen and 3 secondary metabolites were common differential metabolites across the two comparison cohorts (AD-vehicle vs. WT, AD-hucMSC-exosome vs. AD-vehicle), and their aberrant expression in AD mice was all reversed by hucMSC-exosomes. KEGG enrichment analysis showed that hucMSC-exosomes largely reversed dysregulated metabolic pathways in AD, including lipid, amino acid, nucleotide metabolism and autophagy/mitophagy. Collectively, hucMSC-exosomes ameliorate AD pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits, an effect accompanied by metabolic homeostasis remodeling through cascades of reduced Aβ deposition, suppressed neuroinflammation and alleviated oxidative stress. Metabolic remodeling represents a prominent correlative feature of the neuroprotective effects of hucMSC-exosomes, providing candidate molecular targets for metabolically targeted AD therapy.

title: Mitochondrial quality-control states in cadmium neurotoxicity: Adaptive clearance, disproportionate elimination and stalled flux.
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) is a persistent environmental toxicant associated with neurological injury, but the role of mitophagy remains unresolved because increased pathway markers may indicate protective clearance, broad mitochondrial selection or incomplete downstream degradation. This review evaluates mitochondrial quality-control checkpoints in Cd-exposed neural systems, focusing on PINK1-Parkin, BNIP3L/NIX and autophagy-lysosome completion, and examines intervention evidence from puerarin, daidzein and ginsenoside Rg1. Three states are proposed as a conceptual synthesis: adaptive clearance, candidate disproportionate mitochondrial elimination and initiated but stalled flux. Protective PINK1- and BNIP3L-dependent activity has loss-of-function support, whereas selection-pathway engagement accompanied by mitochondrial loss is consistent with, but does not establish, disproportionate elimination because degradation and replacement have not been measured together. Cd also disrupts trafficking, autophagosome-lysosome fusion, lysosomal integrity and proteolysis, providing stronger evidence for incomplete bulk autophagic processing than for mitochondria-specific stalled flux. Among the compounds examined, puerarin has the broadest checkpoint coverage, largely from related cortical studies, linking reduced Cd burden and mitochondrial stress with pool preservation and improved bulk autophagic processing. Evidence for daidzein remains marker-limited, whereas Rg1 protects neuronal and glial endpoints without an established Cd-specific mitochondrial quality-control mechanism. This narrative, non-systematic synthesis is limited by potential selection bias, reliance on static markers, dominance of acute or high-dose exposure models, limited measurement of mitochondria-specific degradation and replacement, inadequate cell-type resolution and scarce independent replication. Resolving these states requires mitochondria-specific flux reporters, direct degradation and replacement indices, causal pathway perturbation and matched Cd and compound exposure. Therapeutic benefit is more likely to arise from restoring selective, proportionate and completed mitochondrial turnover balanced by replacement than from uniformly activating or suppressing mitophagy.

title: Altered developmental trajectories in neurodevelopmental disorders: mechanisms, human models and translational perspectives.
abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are clinically and genetically heterogeneous conditions often studied through diagnostic categories, causal genes, synaptic dysfunction or end-stage phenotypes. Although these approaches remain essential, they do not fully capture the developmental nature of NDD pathophysiology. This review proposes a trajectory-first framework in which NDDs are interpreted as disorders of altered developmental progression. From this perspective, the key question is not only which gene, pathway, cell type, or synapse is affected, but when, where and how neurodevelopment begins to diverge. We discuss mechanisms of trajectory divergence, including altered developmental timing, cell-state and lineage disruption, selective cellular vulnerability, epigenetic and signaling dysregulation, cytoskeletal and morphogenetic abnormalities, synaptic maturation defects, excitability changes and network-level alterations. We then examine how human systems, including fetal and post-mortem atlases, iPSC-derived models, cortical organoids, assembloids, functional readouts and patient-level phenotypes, can be integrated to reconstruct developmental trajectories across biological scales. Representative NDD genes and syndromes illustrate that distinct divergence points may later converge on shared functional or clinical outcomes, including altered excitation/inhibition balance, abnormal network activity, epilepsy, language delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder features or motor dysfunction. Finally, we discuss limitations and perspectives for trajectory-based stratification and biomarker discovery. Rather than acting as static diagnostic readouts, future biomarkers should aim to capture developmental state, timing, divergence, convergence, compensation and response to intervention.
