title: Macamide B alleviates neuronal pyroptosis in spinal cord injury by activating acid ceramidase to inhibit lysosome membrane permeabilization.
abstract: Spinal cord injury is a devastating neurological disorder that causes severe and persistent functional deficits, for which effective pharmacological treatments remain limited. Acid ceramidase is a key lysosomal hydrolase involved in sphingolipid metabolism and has been implicated in cellular homeostasis and central nervous system disorders. However, its role in lysosomal membrane permeabilization and autophagic flux following spinal cord injury remains unclear. In this study, virtual screening identified macamide B as a potential activator of acid ceramidase, and its neuroprotective effects and underlying mechanisms were investigated in a mouse model of spinal cord injury. We found that macamide B treatment significantly reduced glial scar formation and motor neuron loss, thereby improving functional recovery after spinal cord injury. Moreover, macamide B suppressed neuronal pyroptosis and restored impaired autophagic flux associated with lysosomal membrane permeabilization. Mechanistically, macamide B activated acid ceramidase through the extracellular signal-regulated kinase/mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway, thereby alleviating lysosomal membrane permeabilization and restoring autophagic flux, ultimately attenuating neuronal pyroptosis and neuronal loss. Collectively, these findings reveal an extracellular signal-regulated kinase/mitogen-activated protein kinase/acid ceramidase-mediated mechanism underlying the neuroprotective effects of macamide B after spinal cord injury and suggest that pharmacological activation of acid ceramidase may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for promoting neurological recovery following spinal cord injury.

title: Postsynaptic remodeling and F-actin dysregulation in the Dctn1Δ2-4 mouse model of motor neuron disease.
abstract: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons. The dynactin subunit p150Glued, encoded by DCTN1, is associated with motor neuron disease. The p150Glued G59S mutation disrupts the microtubule-binding domain and drives selective motor neuron degeneration in patients and animal models. The p150Glued microtubule-binding domain mediates the initiation of retrograde transport at axonal terminals and stabilizes presynaptic sites at neuromuscular junctions. Nevertheless, the key functions of p150Glued and its microtubule-binding domain within postsynaptic compartments remain poorly defined. Using Dctn1Δ2-4 mice, in which exons 2-4 of Dctn1 encoding the microtubule-binding domain are deleted, we performed morphological, biochemical, and cellular physiological analyses, together with genetic manipulation and pharmacological intervention, to investigate how loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function affects excitatory postsynaptic organization and neuronal vulnerability. We found that excitatory postsynaptic remodeling occurred before overt dendritic degeneration and motor neuron loss in Dctn1Δ2-4 mice. We further demonstrated that p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction induced early remodeling of excitatory postsynaptic densities, leading to increased postsynaptic accumulation of N-methyl- D-aspartate receptors, dysregulated Ca2+ homeostasis, and heightened susceptibility to glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Mechanistically, p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction promoted the postsynaptic accumulation of endosomes and the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog complex, resulting in excessive F-actin assembly and pathological enhancement of postsynaptic density architecture. Furthermore, these postsynaptic abnormalities were rescued by re-expression of wild-type p150Glued, but not the disease-associated G59S mutant. Pharmacological inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, in turn, attenuated excitotoxic injury and neurodegeneration. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized postsynaptic pathogenic mechanism in DCTN1-associated motor neuron disease. We propose that loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function disrupts postsynaptic endosome positioning, leading to aberrant Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog-mediated F-actin remodeling, pathological enhancement of excitatory postsynaptic densities, excessive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor targeting, and increased vulnerability to excitotoxicity.

title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

title: 53BP1 as a cofactor in the activation of the p53-family transcriptional program: A correlative multimodal microscopy approach.
abstract: Understanding how molecular mechanisms regulate cell function in tissues requires approaches that link phenotypes to mechanisms across different spatial scales. Here, we present automated multimodal multiplexed microscopy for image cytometry (A.M3.I.CO), a correlative imaging platform that combines multiscale resolution, from millimeters to nanometers, with automated workflows for high-throughput phenotypic profiling and targeted single-molecule analysis in situ. Applying A.M3.I.CO, we observed that 53BP1 is recruited at transcribed p53 target genes independently of the activating stimulus, providing evidence for the formation of a putative complex between 53BP1, p53, and the basal transcription machinery in single cells, as also supported by in vivo observations in tumor models. Extending our measurements to p63 and p73, we found that 53BP1 localized at p63- and p73-targeted transcription sites, suggesting a broader role in participating in p53 family-dependent transcription. These findings indicate an additional genome-surveillance pathway in transcriptional control regulating diverse cellular functions while establishing A.M3.I.CO as a platform for spatially resolved functional analysis.

title: Chronic thoracic aortitis versus primary medial degeneration in ascending aorta: a digital morphometric analysis of aortic layers remodelling.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chronic aortitis (CA) represents a diverse group of inflammatory conditions often diagnosed incidentally in ascending aorta biopsies. While the 2015 and 2016 Consensus Statements on the surgical pathology of the aorta provide standardised histological classifications, data quantifying structural remodelling within individual aortic layers remain limited. Furthermore, distinguishing CA from primary non-inflammatory medial degeneration (MD) can be challenging, particularly when inflammation is sparse or burnt out, and secondary degenerative changes predominate. We aimed to compare morphological changes in CA and MD aneurysms and apply digital image analysis to quantify aortic wall layers. METHODS: Retrospective histological analysis was performed on 63 ascending aortic specimens: CA (n=21), MD (n=21), and autopsy controls (n=21). Digitised elastic-stained sections were analysed using QuPath software to measure the thickness and cross-sectional area of the intima (I), media (M), and adventitia (A). Overall MD scores (i.e., summaries of each MD grade component) were evaluated. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis based on binary logistic regression models. RESULTS: CA demonstrated a profound architectural shift, characterised by medial thinning alongside marked intimal and adventitial expansion, resulting in significantly lower M/(I+A) thickness and area ratios compared with MD and controls (p <0.001). CA specimens also exhibited the most severe secondary degenerative changes, with significantly higher overall MD scores (median: 15 vs. 8; p < 0.001). ROC curve analysis revealed diagnostic utility of both the M/(I+A) thickness ratio (AUC = 0.964) and the M/(I+A) area ratio (AUC = 0.955) for identifying CA. A multivariable model combining the overall MD score with the M/(I+A) thickness ratio achieved an AUC of 0.971 (accuracy 88.1%), whereas combining it with the M/(I+A) area ratio yielded an AUC of 0.968 (accuracy 90.5%). CONCLUSION: Digital morphometric analysis provides a reproducible and feasible method for quantifying structural remodelling in chronic aortitis. Changes in the proportions of the aortic layers, specifically intimal and adventitial expansion combined with medial thinning and severe secondary medial degeneration, can facilitate accurate differentiation of aortic wall pathologies, particularly in cases with sparse inflammation.

title: Protective role of Galectin-3 in prion disease through regulation of microglial PrPSc uptake.
abstract: Microglia constitute a major innate defense mechanism against prion infection; however, the molecular pathways regulating microglial responses during disease progression remain incompletely understood. Galectin-3 (Gal3), a β-galactoside-binding lectin associated with reactive microglia in multiple neurodegenerative disorders, has been implicated in phagocytosis, inflammatory signaling, and lysosomal homeostasis. Here, we investigated the role of Gal3 in prion disease pathogenesis using prion-infected mice. Gal3 expression was undetectable in healthy brain but became upregulated beginning at late preclinical stages, increasing with disease progression. Gal3 localized predominantly to a subpopulation of reactive IBA1-positive microglia, particularly within the thalamus, and inversely correlated with expression of the homeostatic microglial markers P2Y12 and TMEM119, consistent with acquisition of a reactive phenotype. Microglia engaged in neuronal envelopment displayed elevated Gal3 expression during terminal disease. Constitutive deletion of Gal3 significantly accelerated clinical disease progression without altering total PrPSc accumulation, reactive gliosis, neuronal envelopment, or overall microglial and astrocytic activation. However, Gal3 deficiency markedly reduced microglial uptake of PrPSc, resulting in a lower intracellular-to-extracellular PrPSc ratio, supporting a role for Gal3 in phagocytic sequestration of prions. In contrast, Gal3 deficiency did not impair lysosomal activity, lysosomal membrane integrity, or expression of genes involved in lysosomal repair pathways. Likewise, selective inhibition of autophagy in myeloid cells exerted only minor effects on disease progression. Collectively, these findings identify Gal3 as a sensitive marker of reactive microglia that contributes to microglial uptake of PrPSc and exerts a protective role during prion disease progression.

title: Pathogenesis and therapeutic targets of neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease mediated by microglia lysosomal dysfunction.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two core pathological features: senile plaques formed by amyloid-β protein (Aβ) deposits and neurofibrillary tangles formed by hyperphosphorylated tau protein. In recent years, neuroinflammation has been recognized as a key driver in the pathogenesis of AD, and microglia, as innate immune cells of the central nervous system, play a central role in regulating the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Lysosomes are key organelles within microglia responsible for degrading pathological proteins and regulating inflammatory signaling; dysfunction of lysosomes in microglia severely impairs their ability to clear Aβ, damaged proteins, and cellular debris, thereby promoting inflammatory responses. This manuscript summarizes upstream mechanisms that may influence microglial lysosomal dysfunction from four perspectives: pathological proteins, genetic factors, lipid metabolism disorders, and proinflammatory cytokines. Pathological proteins can impair lysosomal acidification and biogenesis by interfering with key pathways such as the TFEB-v-ATPase axis; various genetic factors exacerbate functional dysregulation by influencing the expression of lysosome-related genes and lipid metabolism; lipid metabolism disorders promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, block the autophagy cascade and activate the inflammasome; proinflammatory cytokines can exert varying effects on the clearance of pathological substrates and by regulating lysosomal function. The aforementioned factors can influence microglial lysosomal function through various mechanisms, thereby contributing to impaired clearance of pathological substrates and the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Intervention strategies targeting microglial lysosomal dysfunction, including enhancing lysosomal degradation capacity, regulating autophagy related pathways, correcting cellular metabolic dysregulation and suppressing excessive neuroinflammation, may offer new avenues for AD treatment.

overview: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two core pathological features: senile plaques formed by amyloid-β protein (Aβ) deposits and neurofibrillary tangles formed by hyperphosphorylated tau protein.

title: The N-Ank protein Ankrd24 shapes neurons and couples to syndapin and the F-actin promoter Cobl-like.
abstract: Proper neuromorphogenesis is pivotal for neuronal network formation and brain function. The underlying cell biological tasks are complex, as they include both remodeling of membrane topologies and of cytoskeletal structures. Yet, mechanisms coordinating these two different cell biological functions are largely unknown. Here, we molecularly and functionally characterize ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 24 (Ankrd24) and demonstrate that this ankyrin-repeat protein is able to interact with and bend membranes and mechanistically and functionally belongs to the recently proposed N-Ank superfamily. Mutational analyses revealed that the N-Ank functions of Ankrd24 are indispensable for Ankrd24's role in neuromorphogenesis. Ankrd24 furthermore physically cooperated with the F-BAR domain protein syndapin I (PACSIN1) and with Cobl-like (Cobll1), a protein promoting actin filament formation, by ternary complex formation. Both partners were critical for Ankrd24-mediated dendritic arborization. This identified Ankrd24 as critical part of a larger, coordinated effort in inducing new dendritic branches. Our work thereby sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the complex task of proper neuronal arbor development.

title: Cross-species molecular mapping of the photoreceptor sensory cilium and periciliary structures identifies conserved and species-specific architectural features.
abstract: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment. The microtubule-based ciliary axoneme extends from the basal body through the connecting cilium into the outer segment, thereby linking the inner and outer segments. Around this central axis, specialized periciliary structures are distributed across the apical inner segment and basal outer segment. Yet how these ciliary and periciliary structures differ between rods and cones and across mammals remains incompletely defined. Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we compared their nanoscale molecular organization across canine, non-human primate and human retinas. Key rod-cone differences in ciliary organization were broadly conserved among all three species, whereas the scale and morphology of individual ciliary subcompartments differed between species. Periciliary structures showed even greater species-specific diversification, particularly in rods. Human photoreceptors shared several structural features with non-human primate photoreceptors but also displayed inter-individual variability in accessory inner segment-like structure. These findings refine current understanding of photoreceptor sensory cilia and associated periciliary structures in large mammals, revealing that conserved rod-cone differences co-exist with pronounced species-specific structural and molecular specializations.

title: A fibril-selective single-domain antibody targets pathogenic amyloid-β assemblies and protects human neurons.
abstract: Alzheimer disease is characterized by extracellular amyloid-β deposition that contributes to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Although anti-amyloid-β antibodies reduce plaque burden, their use requires monitoring for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. Here, phage display against immobilized Aβ40 fibrils representing a patient-relevant polymorph identified J8, a fibril-selective, Fc-free single-domain antibody. J8 bound fibrils with high apparent affinity, showed no detectable binding to monomeric Aβ40, decorated fibril surfaces, and recognized plaque-associated amyloid in Alzheimer disease brain tissue. During concurrent fibril exposure, J8 reduced apoptotic signaling in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and forebrain organoids. Single-nucleus profiling of pooled organoids identified fibril-associated stress programs and opposite-direction expression patterns in the FibJ8 condition; fibril-associated changes showed the strongest directional concordance with advanced disease pathology. These findings identify J8 as a fibril-selective candidate and support organoid-based evaluation of anti-amyloid reagents as a fit-for-purpose preclinical tool.

main: These findings identify J8 as a fibril-selective candidate and support organoid-based evaluation of anti-amyloid reagents as a fit-for-purpose preclinical tool.

title: Protocol for imaging and analyzing the synaptic coverage of astrocytes with super-resolution STED microscopy in mouse brain slices.
abstract: Super-resolution has allowed us to image areas previously inaccessible due to the limits of standard microscopy techniques. Here, we present a protocol to determine the astroglial coverage of synapses. We detail the steps to obtain and label mouse brain slices followed by imaging using 3D stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy and analysis using a custom-made Fiji plug-in, with imaging at a lateral resolution of 80 nm. This technique ascertains the interaction between astrocytes and the glial cell's role in signaling and brain region function.

title: Neuroprotective Effect of Intranasal Breast Milk-Derived Exosomes in a Neonatal Rat Model of Periventricular Leukomalacia.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) is a major cause of neurodevelopmental impairment in premature infants and is characterized by inflammation-associated white matter injury. Breast milk-derived exosomes have regenerative and immunomodulatory properties. METHODS: Experimental PVL was induced in neonatal Sprague-Dawley rats by maternal lipopolysaccharide administration. Animals were assigned to control (n=10), PVL (n=9), PVL + saline (n=10), and PVL + exosome (n=9) groups. Breast milk-derived exosomes were isolated, characterized according to MISEV2018 criteria, and administered intranasally on postnatal days 1, 3, and 5. Histopathological and biochemical analyses were performed on postnatal day 7. RESULTS: Significant differences were observed among groups in microcystic injury, myelin basic protein (MBP) staining, and tyrosine hydroxylase staining (p<0.05). Exosome treatment reduced microcystic white matter injury and preserved MBP staining intensity compared with untreated PVL groups. Tyrosine hydroxylase staining was also higher in the exosome-treated group. No significant differences were observed in GFAP staining intensity, histopathological inflammation scores, or IL-6 levels. IL-1β and TNF-α showed altered profiles, suggesting immunomodulatory effects. PKH26 labeling demonstrated exosome-associated fluorescence in the frontal cortex and hippocampus after intranasal administration. CONCLUSIONS: Intranasal breast milk-derived exosomes attenuated white matter injury and preserved markers of myelin and neuronal integrity in experimental PVL, supporting further investigation in larger models with functional outcome assessments. These findings support a potential cell-free neuroprotective strategy for inflammation-associated neonatal brain injury. However, the use of human breast milk-derived exosomes in rats and the absence of long-term functional outcomes warrant further comparative and longitudinal studies before clinical translation.

title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-h continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

title: Cucurbituril-modulated NIR emission and two-photon mitochondrial imaging of an acridine derivative.
abstract: Host-guest assemblies of an acridine dye with cucurbit[7]uril and cucurbit[8]uril give distinct NIR emissions at 674 and 708 nm, respectively. Both exhibit efficient two-photon absorption near 925 nm and successfully enable single- and two-photon mitochondrial imaging in live A549 cells.
authors: Lin X, Wu J, Shen FF, Duan LT, Wang S, Zhang ZL, Chen KH, Yu HJ, Song R

title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10-9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

title: A seamless workflow for STXM-NEXAFS data analysis using napari: implementation of an ROI spectrum extraction function.
abstract: Scanning transmission soft X-ray microscopy (STXM), combined with near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS), enables the mapping of elemental distributions and chemical properties at a spatial resolution of tens of nanometers. A common approach for analyzing STXM data is to compare NEXAFS spectra obtained from regions of interest (ROIs). However, ROI-based spectral comparison typically requires frequent switching among multiple software applications. ROI spectrum extraction, spectrum normalization, and figure creation are often performed using separate applications, which increase analytical time and the likelihood of errors.•We developed a Python-based workflow for STXM-NEXAFS data analysis that implements functions for extracting mean ROI spectra in napari, an open-source multidimensional image viewer.•These napari-based functions provide a seamless workflow from ROI selection to figure preparation within Python, without switching between multiple software applications.•The seamless workflow improves analytical efficiency and facilitates broader use of STXM-NEXAFS analysis.

title: Six3 promoting the migration and neural differentiation of BMSCs via Btg2‑mediated Akt signaling pathway activation: A therapeutic strategy for stroke.
abstract: Bone marrow‑derived mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) transplantation holds therapeutic potential for stroke; however, but its effectiveness requires optimization. The transcription factor Sine Oculis Homeobox Homolog 3 (Six3) regulates processes crucial for BMSC therapy, such as neural cell proliferation and differentiation. However, whether Six3‑modified BMSCs exert enhanced therapeutic effects on stroke remains unknown. In the present study, mouse BMSCs were isolated and identified using surface markers. Six3‑overexpressing BMSCs exhibited enhanced proliferative, migratory and neural differentiation capacities. RNA‑sequencing analysis comparing the gene expression profiles of BMSCs with and without Six3 overexpression identified BTG Anti‑Proliferation Factor 2 (Btg2) as an upregulated gene (log2FC=1.45, P<0.05) in Six3‑overexpressing cells. Further investigations revealed that Six3 directly binds to the TGATACTGTCT sequence within the Btg2 promoter and activates its transcription. Btg2 knockdown abolished the effects of Six3 overexpression. Mechanistically, Six3 promoted Akt phosphorylation via Btg2, enhancing BMSC viability and neural differentiation. A mouse model of stroke was established using transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO, 1.5‑h occlusion and 24‑h reperfusion). BMSCs were administered via tail vein injection at the onset of reperfusion. GFP expression detected in brain tissue at 24 h post‑reperfusion confirmed successful the homing of BMSCs to the brain. The transplantation of Six3‑overexpressing BMSCs ameliorated brain pathology, reducing apoptosis and cerebral infarct volume. Notably, Six3‑modified BMSCs demonstrated a significantly greater therapeutic efficacy than unmodified BMSCs. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that Six3 enhances the therapeutic properties of BMSCs by transcriptionally activating Btg2, which promotes Akt phosphorylation. These findings provide novel mechanistic insight into the optimization of stem cell therapy in stroke.

title: Extended field-of-view two-photon imaging in the deep brain of freely behaving mice using lightweight microfabricated corrective optics.
abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

title: Unraveling the Genotype-Phenotype Landscape of Kleefstra Syndrome Through EHMT1 Variant Analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Kleefstra syndrome type 1 (KLEFS1) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in EHMT1, which play a key role in epigenetic regulation. Core features include global developmental delay (GDD), intellectual disability (ID), facial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects (CHDs), and neuropsychiatric manifestations. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with KLEFS1 evaluated at Seoul National University Hospital between January 2022 and April 2025. Genetic diagnoses were made using chromosomal microarray or whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, and clinical data were extracted from medical records. To enhance statistical power, we conducted a joint analysis with established cohorts of at least 30 clinically characterized patients. RESULTS: Among the 15 patients with KLEFS1, 14 (93.3%) exhibited GDD or ID, with frequent comorbidities such as CHDs (8/12, 66.7%), orthopaedic manifestations (6/12, 50.0%), epilepsy (6/15, 40.0%), and sleep problems (4/11, 36.4%). Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in 10 of the 12 patients (83.3%), including pituitary anomalies in 2 (16.7%). By combining our data with recently published multicenter international cohorts, we assessed genotype-phenotype correlations by comparing the clinical features of 202 patients with different variant subtypes. Patients with multigene deletions had a significantly higher prevalence of CHDs (53.5% vs 25.8%, p value = 2 × 10-4), cortical visual impairment (12.5% vs 1.7%, p value = 0.004), microcephaly (37.1% vs 17.8%, p value = 0.009), corpus callosum abnormalities (17.9% vs 5.9%, p value = 0.02), and hearing impairment (39.7% vs 25.6%, p value = 0.04) than those with single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) or short insertions/deletions (indels), in addition to the previously identified features including epilepsy, constipation, and short stature. We also observed that a recurrent EHMT1 variant (p.Arg948Trp), identified in multiple unrelated patients, was linked to significant phenotypic heterogeneity, including late-onset neurocognitive regression. DISCUSSION: Our study showed that patients with multigene deletions are significantly more likely to exhibit multiorgan involvement, including CHDs, cortical visual impairments, microcephaly, corpus callosum abnormalities, and hearing impairments, compared with those with SNVs or indels, emphasizing the importance of genotype-informed management. We report pituitary gland abnormalities in KLEFS1, expanding the phenotypic and neuroimaging spectrum of KLEFS1. The patient showing regression in their 30s necessitates long-term, comprehensive studies to support care.

title: Multi-region transcriptomics and unsupervised clustering reveal recurrent and region-specific gene signatures in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits anatomically heterogeneous transcriptomic alterations, complicating the identification of disease-associated genes with consistent external support. We compared four gene-prioritization strategies, absolute log₂ fold change, false discovery rate (FDR), CombinedScore, and RankSum, using laser-capture-microdissected neuronal expression profiles from six brain regions in GSE5281. Differential expression was assessed separately within each region using limma, followed by within-region gene prioritization and cross-region comparison to identify recurrent and anatomically specific candidates. Robustness was evaluated through resampling stability, sensitivity to candidate-list size and scoring formulation, and external benchmarking in three anatomically matched regions of GSE48350. STAT4, SST, and NVL emerged as recurrent candidates, whereas ZNRD2, ANKRD12, and NME7 were prominent regionally prioritized signals. External directional agreement across Top-100 lists ranged from 68.3% to 72.0%; RankSum achieved 71.7% agreement and the highest or joint-highest directional agreement at Top-50 and Top-200. A fixed expression score comprising the three recurrent genes showed higher values in AD in the external cohort. Exploratory six-gene clustering revealed diagnosis-associated structure with modest separation. 14 of 18 gene-region comparisons showed concordant AD-control directions, although cross-dataset effect-size correlations were weak. This study establishes a comparative framework linking regional gene prioritization with stability assessment and independent-cohort benchmarking, identifying recurrent AD-associated candidates and quantifying their external support.

title: Mitochondrial apoptosis imaged by high-throughput confocal microscopy.
abstract: Mitochondrial programmed cell death (i.e. intrinsic apoptosis) is regulated through the formation of pro-apoptotic protein complexes at the mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM), which permeabilize the MOM and commit the cell to die. This step is modulated by mitochondrial dynamics. To capture this, we treated cells with the mitochondrial dynamics inhibitor M1 before inducing apoptosis with actinomycin D (ActD), and imaged them by high-throughput spinning-disk confocal microscopy. In mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) we followed apoptosis by long-term live-cell imaging, and in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) we stained fixed cells for the pro-apoptotc protein BAX at mitochondria. Here, we provide a description of these two large-scale microscopy datasets. Dataset 1 contains 637,632 images of MEFs imaged as time series after labelling of mitochondrial morphology and integrity with the mitochondrial membrane potential-sensitive dye tetramethylrhodamine-ethylester (TMRE) and apoptosis with Annexin V-FITC. The dataset also contains a digital phase contrast channel which can be useful to track cells. Dataset 2 contains 9,504 images of hiPSCs with immunofluorescence labelling of BAX and COX IV. The datasets are made available through the BioImage Archive repository.

title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

title: Impaired autophagy and lysosome function in human fibroblast aging.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Human aging is characterized by a progressive, time-dependent deterioration in physiological and cognitive functioning. Aging is driven by an array of interconnected cellular hallmarks, including genomic instability, mitochondrial dysfunction, telomere attrition, epigenetic alteration and dysfunctional autophagy. Autophagy is a cytoprotective (cellular degradation and recycling) pathway that maintains homeostasis during starvation or stress, and whose activity is associated with extended lifespan. This multi-step process comprises autophagosome formation and maturation, autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and cargo degradation. Thus, analysis of autophagy flux is necessary to precisely design therapeutic interventions aimed at restoring autophagy in aging. METHODS: The autophagy flux was comprehensively analyzed in human skin fibroblasts from donors of different ages (20-96 years old), a cell system that retains age-associated cellular and molecular signatures. The subcellular localization and activity of the master transcription factor of autophagy and lysosome biogenesis, TFEB, was analyzed by confocal microscopy assays and transcriptional expression of TFEB target genes (RT-qPCR) respectively. The autophagy flux was evaluated by monitoring the autophagy markers LC3 and p62 by Western blotting and confocal microscopy analyses, using inhibitor drugs to block autophagy or lysosomal activity. Autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion were analyzed by colocalizing LC3 with Sintaxin-17 and LC3 with the lysosomal protein LAMP1 respectively, using inhibitor drugs and confocal microscopy assays. The analysis of lysosomal morphology and function was evaluated by lysobrite dye staining and live-cell confocal microscopy analysis. RESULTS: The initial stages of autophagy, including activation of TFEB, and autophagosome formation, remained apparently functional in fibroblast aging. In contrast, the rate of both autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion, as well as the lysosomal function appears to be altered in aged fibroblasts. Specifically, enlarged dysfunctional lysosomes were identified as a hallmark of the fibroblasts of the 96-year-old donor. This lysosomal dysfunction may lead to a reduced ability to degrade canonical autophagy markers, LC3-II and p62, and the accumulation of lipofuscin. CONCLUSION: Overall, the results provide evidence that autophagy flux is impaired at the late stages in aged fibroblasts, specifically in autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion steps. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that this failure correlates with the presence of enlarged dysfunctional lysosomes. This study underscores the significance of enhancing lysosomal activity to counteract autophagy decline in aging.

title: MD2-IN-1 restores microglial lysosomal function and attenuates amyloid pathology through TREM2-associated signaling in 5×FAD mice.
abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a central regulator of microglial adaptation during Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the development of small-molecule modulators associated with TREM2 signaling remains limited. Here, through a consensus pharmacophore-guided virtual screening strategy, MD2-IN-1 was identified as a candidate small molecule associated with TREM2 signaling. Biolayer interferometry and cellular thermal shift assays supported cellular target engagement related to TREM2 (KD = 13.85 μM). In Aβ-stimulated BV2 microglia, MD2-IN-1 increased SYK phosphorylation, promoted Aβ uptake, and shifted microglial responses toward a less proinflammatory phenotype. These effects were markedly attenuated following Trem2 knockdown, indicating the involvement of the TREM2-SYK signaling pathway. Mechanistically, MD2-IN-1 restored lysosomal acidification and increased the expression of the V-ATPase subunits ATP6v0c and ATP6v0a1, accompanied by increased intracellular Aβ degradation. In 5×FAD mice, chronic MD2-IN-1 administration improved cognitive performance without detectable behavioral abnormalities compared with WT animals. Multimodal PET imaging demonstrated reduced amyloid deposition and attenuated neuroinflammatory signals, which were further supported by histological analyses showing decreased plaque burden, reduced inflammatory microglial responses, and preserved neuronal integrity. In addition, MD2-IN-1 reduced P62 accumulation and restored ATP6v0c expression in vivo, whereas these effects were partially attenuated by pharmacological inhibition of TREM2. Collectively, these findings identify MD2-IN-1 as a small-molecule modulator associated with TREM2 signaling that restores microglial lysosomal degradative function and promotes Aβ clearance in AD models, providing pharmacological support for targeting adaptive microglial responses in AD.

title: Beyond PROTACs: Conditional Technologies and New Frontiers.
abstract: This chapter surveys the post-PROTAC landscape of targeted protein degradation (TPD), covering conditional activation, new degradation modalities, and proximity-driven editing of post-translational modifications (PTMs). Condition-activated PROTACs harness prodrugs responsive to irradiation or the tumor microenvironment and nanoparticle-based platforms to achieve spatiotemporally resolved protein degradation. The targetable space is further expanded by molecular glues that recruit neosubstrates to E3 ligases, endocytosis-lysosome targeting chimeras that clear extracellular and membrane proteins, and autophagy-lysosome strategies that degrade aggregates and damaged organelles. Ribonuclease-recruiting chimeras achieve targeted RNA degradation, while the induced-proximity concept is repurposed for PTM regulation, enabling targeted glycosylation, acetylation, and phosphorylation and dephosphorylation via the recruitment of glycosyltransferases, acetyltransferases, and kinases and phosphatases. Future advances in all-small-molecule-based conditional systems, brain-targeted delivery, and regulatory frameworks informed by degradation kinetics will embed stimulus sensing and logic-gated operations into intelligent molecular systems, shifting the paradigm toward on-demand proteome and transcriptome rewiring for precision medicine.

title: Levetiracetam restores GABAergic function and network homeostasis following Vps35 deficiency in excitatory neurons.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRDs) remain incurable, partly due to their complex and poorly understood pathogenic mechanisms. Loss of vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein 35 (VPS35), a core component of the retromer complex, has been implicated in AD and ADRDs. While Vps35 deficiency is known to increase amyloidogenesis by regulating its cargo proteins, such as APP and BACE1, the precise mechanism by which VPS35 dysfunction leads to cognitive impairment remains elusive. While neuronal VPS35 regulates trafficking and functions of multiple synaptic membrane proteins, such as postsynaptic glutamatergic and GABAnergic receptors and pre-synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, and Levetiracetam (LEV), an antiepileptic drug that improves cognition, interacts with the SV2A, exactly how LEV enhances cognition is still a matter of debate. METHODS: Given the abundant expression of VPS35 in pyramidal excitatory neurons, we generated a conditional knockout mouse model with Vps35 deletion from postnatal glutamatergic excitatory neurons (Vps35CaMKIIα) and characterized its phenotypes using a combination of behavioral assessments, and electrophysiological, biochemical, and immunohiotological analyses in the hippocampal CA1 region. A targeted pharmacological screen was conducted to evaluate the therapeutic potential of LEV. RESULTS: Vps35 deletion did not disrupt the gross brain development but led to progressive cognitive decline beginning at three months of age. Electrophysiological analyses revealed earlier-onset hippocampal CA1 hyperexcitability, marked by depolarized resting membrane potentials and reduced Kir2.1 expression. However, restoring Kir2.1 to suppress hyperexcitability failed to rescue cognitive deficits. Instead, cognitive impairment was associated with weakened GABAergic transmission and disruption of the excitatory/inhibitory balance in the Schaffer collateral-CA1 circuit. Notably, LEV treatment diminished these deficits in mutant mice. Intriguingly, LEV increased the levels of retromer component, VPS26A, and multiple pre- and postsynaptic GABAergic proteins, in addition to SV2A, all of which were reduced in Vps35-deficient CA1 neurons. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify VPS35 in excitatory neurons as a critical factor for inhibitory synapse maintenance and network homeostasis. This study also highlights LEV as a potential therapeutic strategy for ADRDs through the preservation of GABAergic synapses.

title: Low-dose radiotherapy ameliorates Alzheimer's-like pathology in 5xFAD mice and is associated with HIF-1α-related inflammatory signaling downregulation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether fractionated low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) alleviates Alzheimer's disease-like pathology and whether these effects are associated with microglial HIF-1α-related signaling remain unclear. METHODS: Male 5xFAD mice received whole-brain irradiation at 2 Gy per fraction for 5 fractions (total dose, 10 Gy). One month later, cognition was assessed by the Morris water maze and novel object recognition tests, and brain pathology was evaluated by immunofluorescence and Western blot. LPS-stimulated BV2 cells were used as an in vitro model to examine the effects of LDRT on nitric oxide, cytokines, and reactive oxygen species. Transcriptomic analysis was performed with 3 biological replicates per group, followed by pharmacological validation using the HIF-1α inhibitor YC-1. RESULTS: LDRT improved spatial and recognition memory, reduced Aβ plaque burden in the hippocampus and cortex, and attenuated microglial activation in 5xFAD mice. In particular, LDRT decreased the hippocampal Aβ plaque area fraction (P = 0.0065) and reduced HIF-1α expression in Iba1-positive microglia in the hippocampus (P = 0.0077). In addition, LDRT reduced Iba1 expression and CD68-positive area while preserving Aβ phagocytosis by primary microglia. In BV2 cells, LDRT inhibited LPS-induced inflammatory responses and altered 123 differentially expressed genes enriched in the HIF-1, IL-17, TNF, MAPK, and p53 signaling pathways. Pharmacological inhibition of HIF-1α by YC-1 recapitulated, but did not further enhance, the anti-inflammatory effects of LDRT. CONCLUSIONS: Fractionated whole-brain LDRT ameliorates cognitive deficits and Aβ pathology in 5xFAD mice, with effects associated with downregulation of microglial HIF-1α-related signaling.

title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34-45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. Collectively, our findings suggest that the epitope accessibility and topology of EV-associated αSyn proteoforms, rather than their abundance alone, discriminate synucleinopathy subtypes, offering a framework for a blood-based conformational stratification of these disorders.

title: The small giant actor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases: Microtubules.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a clinically and pathologically diverse group of disorders characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment, and neuronal loss. Although research has traditionally focused on disease-associated protein misfolding and aggregation, increasing evidence implicates abnormalities of cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport in several neurodegenerative conditions. Microtubules contribute to neuronal polarity, axonal and dendritic transport, organelle distribution, and synaptic maintenance. These functions are regulated in part by tubulin isotypes, post-translational modifications collectively described as the tubulin code, microtubule-associated proteins, and molecular motors. This narrative review examines evidence linking alterations in these processes with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease. We summarize proposed interactions among microtubule instability, impaired axonal transport, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disease-associated proteins, including tau, α-synuclein, mutant huntingtin, TDP-43, and prion protein. Evidence connecting tau pathology with microtubule dysfunction is comparatively well established in Alzheimer's disease and MAPT-related tauopathies, whereas findings in other disorders are more heterogeneous and are frequently derived from cellular or animal models. We also discuss emerging experimental approaches, candidate biomarkers, and investigational microtubule-directed treatments. However, no tubulin-specific biomarker or microtubule-targeted disease-modifying treatment discussed in this review has yet been clinically validated. Overall, microtubule dysfunction may represent one component of broader, disease-specific pathological networks rather than a universal primary cause of neurodegeneration. Further longitudinal and clinical studies are needed to determine whether microtubule-related alterations act as causes, consequences, or modifiers of disease progression.

title: Endosome-associated Rab GTPases control distinct aspects of neural circuit assembly.
abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

title: CHCHD2 mitigates age-associated proteostatic collapse by maintaining homeostasis of the mitochondria-lysosome axis.
abstract: Mutations in coiled-coil-helix-coiled-coil-helix domain containing 2 (CHCHD2), including the Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked CHCHD2T61I mutation, are associated with Lewy body disorders (LBDs) by unknown mechanisms. Here, we demonstrate that CHCHD2T61I exacerbates age-related brain pathologies, including axonal degeneration and cognitive deficits, by disrupting the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Specifically, CHCHD2T61I binds and reduces cathepsin B (CTSB) and cathepsin L (CTSL) levels, inducing lysosomal membrane permeability and impairing α-synuclein fibril clearance. We also demonstrate that human CHCHD2 declines in the brain with age, while expression of wild-type CHCHD2 safeguards against age-related neuroinflammation, dopaminergic neuron loss, insoluble protein aggregation, and structural deterioration of mitochondria and lysosomes. These findings, supported by observed reductions in CTSB and CHCHD2 in human LBD brains, establish CHCHD2 as a key regulator of neuronal resilience to aging and proteostatic collapse via the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Preventing age-associated CHCHD2 decline offers a therapeutic strategy to preserve brain health throughout aging.

title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

title: Beyond cell replacement: restoring organelle homeostasis as the next frontier of regenerative medicine.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) have traditionally been viewed as disorders driven by individual pathological processes, including protein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, impaired autophagy, and neuroinflammation. However, growing evidence demonstrates that these mechanisms are not isolated events but interconnected manifestations of disrupted intracellular organelle communication. Dynamic interactions among mitochondria, the ER, lysosomes, peroxisomes, and other organelles coordinate calcium signaling, bioenergetics, proteostasis, lipid metabolism, and cellular stress adaptation, thereby preserving neuronal homeostasis. Progressive disruption of this communication network represents a fundamental driver of neuronal dysfunction and degeneration, suggesting that restoration of organelle homeostasis may constitute a more effective therapeutic strategy than targeting individual molecular pathways. In parallel, regenerative medicine has evolved beyond the concept of cell replacement toward approaches that enhance the resilience and repair capacity of surviving cells. Among these, mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived secretomes and extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as promising cell-free therapeutics owing to their diverse repertoire of proteins, lipids, metabolites, cytokines, growth factors, and regulatory RNAs capable of simultaneously modulating multiple cellular pathways. Accumulating evidence indicates that these bioactive cargos modulate mitochondrial function, alleviate ER stress, improve autophagy-lysosomal activity, reduce oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, and reinforce proteostasis, collectively promoting intracellular homeostasis. Here, we propose organelle homeostasis as a promising focus for regenerative medicine and discuss how cell-free therapies may redefine therapeutic strategies for NDs by restoring the intracellular communication networks that sustain cellular resilience. Finally, we highlight current translational challenges and future opportunities for engineering next-generation cell-free therapeutics targeting complex diseases.

title: Early-life exposure to environmental pollutants and endocrine disruptors: emerging risks and mechanistic insights in maternal, fetal, and child health.
abstract: Exposure to environmental pollutants and endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) in early life is a critical public health issue because it can alter developmental programming that impacts susceptibility to disease throughout life. The prenatal and early postnatal periods are times of vulnerability when exposure to environmental stressors may impact endocrine signalling, placental function, epigenetic regulation, and metabolic homeostasis. There is increasing evidence that exposure to bisphenols, phthalates, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), pesticides, heavy metals, and air pollutants has been associated with pregnancy outcomes, neurodevelopmental disorders, metabolic dysfunction, endocrine abnormalities and reproductive impairments. Exposomics, high-resolution mass spectrometry, biomonitoring, and passive sampling technologies have made crucial advances in characterising complex environmental exposures. At the same time, novel methods such as multi-omics, single-cell sequencing, spatial biology and microbiome studies have yielded more detailed mechanistic understanding of how environmental factors can impact developmental processes via epigenetic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, and endocrine pathways. The placenta has emerged as a valuable biomarker matrix for assessing fetal exposure and developmental programming. Exposure routes, biomonitoring methods, placental processes, molecular and epigenetic modifications, and the impacts of early-life environmental exposures on neurodevelopment, metabolism, endocrine function, and reproduction are all summarised in this review. It also emphasises current advancements in exposure assessment, preventive measures, and policy frameworks, highlighting the importance of life-course perspectives and environmental justice. To identify important windows of susceptibility, improve risk assessment, and develop strategies to safeguard maternal and child health, exposomics in conjunction with systems biology and longitudinal epidemiological approaches will be essential.

title: Human-Derived Motor Neuron Progenitor Cell Implantation Rescues Motor Endplates Following Peripheral Nerve Injury.
abstract: PURPOSE: Degradation of motor endplates (MEPs) following peripheral nerve injury (PNI) is a major determinant of functional recovery, as prolonged denervation renders target muscles progressively unreceptive to reinnervation. While prior studies have demonstrated that stem cell-based therapies may provide neurotrophic support following PNI, their potential effects on MEP preservation have not been well studied. We hypothesized that transplantation of human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived motor neuron progenitors (MNPs) into chronically denervated muscle would be associated with preservation of MEP architecture. METHODS: With Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee approval, chronic denervation injuries were created in mice via sciatic nerve transection. After 4 months of denervation, when MEPs have consistently degraded in this animal model, the denervated tibialis anterior (TA) was injected with low-dose MNPs (10,000 cells), high-dose MNPs (500,000 cells), or phosphate-buffered saline (negative control). Using a previously established method, hiPSCs were differentiated into functional MNPs prior to injection. At selected time points post-injection, the TA was harvested and immunostained to confirm MNP viability and detect the presence of MEPs. RESULTS: Transplanted MNPs remained viable within host muscle at both evaluated time points. No identifiable MEPs were detected in phosphate-buffered saline-treated chronically denervated muscle. In contrast, MNP-treated muscles demonstrated the presence of MEP-like structures following prolonged denervation. Qualitative differences in MEP density and morphologic complexity were observed between treatment groups, with greater preservation seen in the higher-dose cohort. Contralateral uninjured muscles demonstrated intact native MEP architecture. CONCLUSIONS: Intramuscular transplantation of hiPSC-derived MNPs into chronically denervated muscle was associated with preservation of MEP morphology in this preclinical proof-of-concept model. These preliminary findings suggest that cellular therapies may represent a potential adjunctive strategy to preserve end-organ receptivity following delayed peripheral nerve injury. TYPE OF STUDY/LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Preclinical controlled animal study, Level V.

title: TPPU, a soluble epoxide hydrolase inhibitor, mitigates Aβ-induced neurotoxicity via dual modulation of mitochondrial stabilization and JNK suppression.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, primarily driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) aggregation and neuronal apoptosis. This study aims to investigate the neuroprotective effects of soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) inhibition against Aβ-induced cytotoxicity in PC-12 cells, focusing on cell viability, apoptosis, and the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling pathway. Western blotting and fluorometric assays revealed elevated sEH expression and activity in Aβ1-42-treated PC-12 cells compared to untreated controls. Treatment with N-[1-(1-Oxopropyl)-4-piperidinyl]-N'-[4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenyl]urea (TPPU), a potent sEH inhibitor, significantly attenuated Aβ-induced apoptosis in PC-12 cells and enhanced cell viability. These findings were corroborated by CCK-8 assays and flow cytometry analyses. Furthermore, TPPU reversed Aβ-induced cleaved Caspase-3 dysregulation and restored mitochondrial membrane potential. Notably, exogenous administration of epoxyeicosatrienoic acids partially mimicked the protective effects of TPPU, primarily by preserving mitochondrial function. Western blot analysis confirmed that TPPU pretreatment suppressed the phosphorylation of JNK, thereby contributing to its anti-apoptotic effects. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that TPPU attenuates Aβ-induced neurotoxicity via dual mechanisms-restoring mitochondrial function and suppressing JNK activation-highlighting its potential as a therapeutic agent for AD.

title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function. METHODS: We utilized healthy subjects and patients with SMA induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cultures to assess phenotypes occurring intrinsically within astrocyte processes (monocultures) and at the PAP-synaptic interface (co-cultures), respectively, using cell surface capture mass spectrometry proteomics, confocal and super resolution microscopy, synaptogliosome (SG) isolation, and electrophysiology. RESULTS: SMA astrocytes demonstrated intrinsic filopodia actin defects featuring low abundance of actin-associated cell surface N-glycoproteins, decreased filopodia density and CDC42-GTP levels after actin remodeling stimulation, and significantly reduced phosphorylated ezrin, radixin, and moesin (pERM) proteins. Within the SMA motor neuron and astrocyte co-cultures, we observed concurrent decreases in synapse number, actin-associated synapsin I expression, and PAP-associated expression of pERM proteins. Our dual treatment paradigm using SMN1 gene therapy combined with forskolin treatment to stimulate actin dynamics via increasing cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels resulted in increased branching and filopodia density of SMA astrocytes, and improved synapse formation and function of SMA motor neurons. INTERPRETATION: We define actin-associated defects impacting astrocyte filopodia dynamics and motor neuron synaptic function in SMA. This shaped our therapeutic approach targeted to SMN-dependent and actin-related disease mechanisms, which overall demonstrated improvements in motor neuron function and disease pathology. title: KIF1A c.773C > T impairs neural progenitor differentiation and axonal transport in association with dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling.
abstract: Pathogenic KIF1A variants are established cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. However, the mechanisms by which they perturb early human neural development remains undefined. Here, we identified a heterozygous KIF1A c.773C > T (p.T258M) mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary spastic paraplegia and modeled its pathogenicity using patient-derived iPSCs and CRISPR-Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. We found that KIF1A-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) exhibited hyperproliferation, impaired cell-cycle exit, and defective neuronal differentiation, accompanied by defective neurite outgrowth, neuronal complexity, and calcium activity. Mechanistically, the KIF1A c.773C > T mutation compromised the binding affinity of KIF1A for β-tubulin and thereby impaired microtubule-associated localization of BDNF and synaptophysin. Integrated transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Notably, pharmacological activation of Wnt signaling restored BDNF expression, whereas exogenous BDNF rescued the proliferative and differentiative defects, indicating a potential functional relationship between BDNF and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Collectively, these findings suggested that dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling may serve as a contributory mechanism linking KIF1A motor dysfunction to aberrant neural stem cell fate.

title: Time-lapse RESOLFT nanoscopy empowered by deep learning.
abstract: Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

title: Antisense Oligonucleotides that Are Toxic to Prion-Infected Mice Share an Emergent Mechanism.
abstract: Some, but not all, gapmer antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) delivered into cerebrospinal fluid exhibit fatal subacute toxicity in late-stage prion-infected mice but not in uninfected mice. Here, we performed a battery of in vivo studies demonstrating that the toxicity is compound- and disease- stage-dependent, and not predicted by behavioral or molecular measurements in uninfected animals. A panel of toxic ASOs all elicited a consistent transcriptomic response signature in prion-infected mice, which emerged over the course of 7 days post dose. This signature, driven chiefly by decreased expression of a specific set of astrocyte-expressed genes, was absent in uninfected mice receiving the same ASOs, was absent, less intense, and/or more transient in infected mice receiving tolerated ASOs, and was distinct from the transcriptomic effect of prion disease itself. Our data argue that the toxicity is an interaction between ASO and prion disease at high doses for specific compounds, and does not represent an exacerbation of ASO toxicity nor of prion disease.

title: Multiple motor proteins regulate TDP-43 anterograde axonal transport.
abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is an RNA-binding protein essential for RNA metabolism. Under physiological conditions, it predominantly resides in the nucleus but is also expressed in the cytoplasm, where it regulates mRNA trafficking and local translation. In nearly 97% of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases, TDP-43 undergoes nuclear depletion and cytoplasmic aggregation. While its nuclear functions are well characterized, its axonal roles remain poorly understood, despite axonal degeneration being a hallmark of ALS pathology. To address this gap, we investigated TDP-43 localization and transport dynamics in axons of H9-derived human neurons. We compared fluorescently labeled TDP-43 with three well-characterized axonal cargoes, ras-related protein Rab5, synaptophysin, and amyloid precursor protein, and examined protein-protein interactions between TDP-43 and the axonal transport machinery. Our analyses revealed that TDP-43 exhibits active anterograde axonal transport and interacts with multiple kinesin motor proteins, including all three KIF5 isoforms, through the adaptor KLC1, and the synaptic vesicles motor KIF1A. This multi-motor engagement suggests a flexible transport system that ensures mRNA delivery to distal axons. In ALS, where TDP-43 accumulates abnormally in the cytoplasm, this flexibility may become compromised, with multiple transport mechanisms simultaneously affected. This could contribute to progressive accumulation of non-functional TDP-43 granules, disrupting mRNA trafficking and local translation. Our findings provide a foundation for understanding how physiological TDP-43 transport mechanisms may be impaired during disease, highlighting axonal TDP-43 transport pathways as potential therapeutic targets.

title: The postsynaptic scaffold protein ABLIM1 regulates seizure susceptibility by maintaining GluA2 membrane localization in chronic epilepsy.
abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common form of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) in adults, is a frequent chronic neurological disorder. Nevertheless, the precise pathophysiological mechanisms underlying TLE remain largely undefined. Our findings demonstrate that Actin-binding LIM protein 1 (ABLIM1) is broadly expressed in the adult mouse brain, with high expression in the hippocampus. The protein is primarily localized to neurons, enriched in the postsynaptic density (PSD), colocalizes with the scaffold protein PSD95, and directly binds to F-actin. Co-IP experiments confirmed that ABLIM1 interacts with the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) subunits GluA1 and GluA2. Following hippocampal stereotaxic injection of adeno-associated virus (AAV) to specifically knock down ABLIM1 expression, we observed reduced F-actin polymerization, decreased dendritic spine density, and thinning of the PSD in the mouse hippocampus. In the chronic epilepsy models induced by kainic acid (KA), ABLIM1 knockdown significantly exacerbated seizure severity and increased seizure susceptibility. Further mechanistic studies revealed that ABLIM1 knockdown specifically reduces membrane expression of GluA2 without altering its total protein levels. Collectively, ABLIM1 may regulate epileptogenesis and disease progression by maintaining postsynaptic structural integrity and GluA2 membrane homeostasis. Thus, the ABLIM1-GluA2 signaling axis represents a potential therapeutic target for DRE.

title: Dystrophic changes of nigrostriatal axons harboring a SYNJ1 Parkinson's mutation suggest catastrophic failure of endocytic mechanisms.
abstract: Synaptojanin 1 is a brain enriched phosphoinositide phosphatase implicated in endocytosis at the synapse. A mutation (R258Q) that selectively impairs its Sac1 phosphatase domain causes early onset familial Parkinsonism. Neurons of mice with this mutation display synaptic vesicle traffic defects across the brain, but selective dystrophic changes in a subset of dopaminergic axons in the dorsolateral striatum. Using correlative light microscopy-FIB-SEM of mutant mouse striata to visualize in 3D these abnormal structures we show that they represent clusters of focal axonal dilations harboring massive, onion-like DAT enriched plasma membrane infoldings, generally localized next to cell bodies of neighboring cells, often engulfing evaginations of such cells. This dysmorphia was associated with a deficit in dopamine release in the same striatal region. Given the involvement of Synj1 in endocytic mechanisms, these structures may reflect an imbalance between exocytosis and endocytosis. Their occurrence only in a subset of axons suggests a vulnerability threshold of these axons beyond which the expansion of the plasma membrane is not counteracted by compensatory mechanisms.

authors: Wu Y, Xu P, Moran J, Xu CS, Hayworth KJ, Cao M, Shao L, James Surmeier D, Hess HF, De Camilli P
